With that line gone, a listener connection drop while messages are posted means those messages are NEVER pushed to the live handler for the rest of the process's life (only a later NOTIFY for a newer message would pull them in as a side effect). The same suite is also blind to dropping the `this.waiters.keys()` half of the re-LISTEN loop, which would strand every in-flight blocking fetch across a reconnect.
remediation: Extend the existing mocked-pg harness: subscribe, emit 'end' on the listener, queue rows in state.drainRows, let the reconnect complete, and assert (a) the new client received LISTEN for every channel in subs AND waiters, and (b) the queued rows reached the handler without any NOTIFY being emitted.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a recovery/reconnect path is covered only by its negative (must-not-resurrect) assertion, never by the delivery guarantee it exists to provide'. Parameterize a reconnect scenario over (active subscriptions: 0 | 1 | 2 topics) x (in-flight blocking waiters: 0 | 1) x (rows committed during the blackout: 0 | 1 | DRAIN_BATCH+1) and assert, in every cell, exact-once ascending delivery to each handler and prompt release of each waiter. The same generator should be reused for the disconnect-during-reconnect case already covered, so BUG-16 and the delivery guarantee cannot drift apart.

summary: The SEC-06 default-credential warning fires only on exact equality with the literal DSN `postgres://parley:parley@127.0.0.1:5432/parley`. It is a string match, not a credential check — yet the README instructs the operator to provision exactly `POSTGRES_USER=parley / POSTGRES_PASSWORD=parley`, so the common variants of that same repo-public credential pair pass silently.
failure: `backend_config.url: 'postgres://parley:parley@localhost:5432/parley'` (or `@db:5432/parley` in the dev-compose/Docker-network form, or `@127.0.0.1/parley` with the port omitted) -> no warning is printed, even though the credentials are the world-known ones the README's own `docker run` snippet creates. The operator gets an explicit all-clear for a database whose password is published in this repo.
remediation: Parse the DSN and warn on the credential pair (user==='parley' && password==='parley'), independently of host/port/database and of whether url was supplied. Keep the existing 'url unset' warning as a separate case. Consider tightening the README's docker snippet to generate a password rather than hardcoding one.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a security guard asserts a literal string instead of the property it is protecting'. Replace the three-case creds-warning test with a table: [undefined, the exact default, 'postgres://parley:parley@localhost:5432/parley', 'postgres://parley:parley@db/parley', 'postgres://parley:parley@127.0.0.1/other', 'postgres://parley:hunter2@127.0.0.1:5432/parley', 'postgres://app:s3cret@db.example.com:5432/prod'] with an expected warn/no-warn column — every row whose credentials are parley/parley must warn, every other row must not.

summary: bridge-postgres creates and wholly owns its message table, but ships no `retention_days` prune knob — unlike bridge-sqlite, bridge-redis and bridge-nats, which all implement one. DESIGN §11's own stated rule is that the knob belongs on 'the backends whose store Parley itself owns', which is exactly what this table is. The table grows without bound with no documented pruning path.
failure: A long-running deployment on the default `parley_messages` table accumulates every message ever posted, forever. The operator who read DESIGN §11 and set `backend_config.retention_days: 7` (valid on sqlite/redis/nats) gets no error and no pruning — the field is simply ignored by PostgresBackendConfig, which is a silent no-op the surrounding codebase explicitly forbids elsewhere (see the config loader rejecting `backend:` and `skip_permissions: true` rather than ignoring them).
remediation: Either implement retention_days (a periodic `DELETE FROM <t> WHERE ts < now() - interval`, or a documented pg_cron/partitioning pointer in the README), or — at minimum — reject an unknown/unsupported `retention_days` in connect() and state plainly in the README that retention is the operator's job, so the omission is fail-fast rather than a silent no-op. Update DESIGN §11's list either way.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a config field that is meaningful on sibling backends is silently ignored by this one'. Add a cross-package test (or a conformance-factory hook) that, for every backend whose store Parley creates, asserts each documented backend_config key is either honoured or explicitly rejected — never silently dropped. Concretely: a table of {backend, key} pairs derived from DESIGN §11 with an expected disposition column, so adding a backend or a knob forces a decision instead of defaulting to silence.

summary: connect() never settles when the Redis server is unreachable: node-redis v4's default reconnectStrategy retries forever and the swallowing `client.on('error')` handler hides every ECONNREFUSED, so `await client.connect()` stays pending indefinitely.
failure: Input: `backend_config: { url: 'redis://127.0.0.1:6399' }` (typo'd port / Redis not started yet). Reproduced: `plugin.connect(...)` neither resolved nor rejected after 9s of polling (script printed 'still waiting' every 2s and gave up). Wrong output: `parley-redis --config parley.config.yaml` hangs forever inside buildBridge -> plugin.connect; no tools are ever registered, nothing is written to stderr, the process never exits, and Claude Code sees a stdio MCP server that started but never answers initialize. Note the package's own test harness works around exactly this (`isRedisUp` builds its probe client with `socket: { connectTimeout: 800, reconnectStrategy: false }`) while the plugin does not.
remediation: Pass fail-fast socket options for the INITIAL connect: `createClient({ url, socket: { connectTimeout: cfg.connect_timeout_ms ?? 5000, reconnectStrategy: (retries) => (connected ? Math.min(50 * 2 ** retries, 2000) : new Error('parley-redis: cannot reach <url>')) } })` — i.e. give up (reject connect()) before the first successful handshake, keep bounded backoff reconnect afterwards so the outage-recovery behaviour I verified is preserved. Also log the failing URL host:port (never the password) to stderr from cli.ts.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'plugin startup must fail fast, never hang, on an unreachable/wrong endpoint' with a table-driven test in every network backend's suite: for each of [closed port, blackholed IP (e.g. 10.255.255.1 with a short timeout), DNS name that does not resolve, port that accepts TCP but speaks no protocol (a bare net.createServer that never replies)], assert `await expect(plugin.connect(cfg)).rejects.toThrow()` within a bounded `vi.waitFor` deadline. The existing conformance suite can never catch this because it only ever runs when a server is already reachable, and its own reachability probe uses a different client configuration than the plugin.

summary: During a Redis outage, post()/fetchRecent() never reject — node-redis queues commands offline for the whole outage — so `parley_post` / `parley_fetch_recent` tool calls hang for an unbounded time. The comment at the swallowing error handler asserts the opposite ('transient connection errors surface via command rejections'), which is factually wrong.
failure: Input: connect to a live Redis, then kill the server (`redis-cli -p 6390 shutdown nosave`) and call `post(topic,'a','during')` and `fetchRecent({topic})`. Reproduced: neither promise settled after 8s of outage (script printed '8s elapsed, still pending'); in a second run the post resolved only 2768ms later, exactly when I restarted the server. Wrong output: an agent's parley_post hangs for the full length of the outage (minutes/hours) with no error, no timeout and no diagnostic; the presence heartbeat loop stalls the same way, so peers see a stale roster instead of a failure.
remediation: Set `disableOfflineQueue: true` (commands reject immediately with a connection error while disconnected) and/or `commandOptions({ timeout })` / a wrapping `Promise.race` deadline on post/fetchRecent, so callers get a real error they can retry; then fix the comment at src/index.ts:66-68 to state what actually happens (errors are swallowed here and surfaced as command rejections ONLY IF the offline queue is disabled).
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'every seam call must settle (resolve or reject) within a bounded deadline while the backend is down' as a shared, parameterized case in the conformance suite gated on an optional `killBackend()/reviveBackend()` context hook: for each seam method in [post, fetchRecent, fetchRecent-with-blockMs, resolveIdentity, subscribe], kill the server and assert the promise settles within e.g. 2x a declared timeout budget, then revive and assert the plugin recovers. No current test in bridge-redis exercises any backend-down path.

summary: A `since` cursor that points past the stream's last generated id (minted against a different Redis, a re-created dataset, or a peer whose clock is ahead) makes fetchRecent return an empty page forever and echo the stale cursor as nextCursor — catch-up for that topic is silently wedged. bridge-sqlite explicitly fixed this exact class (malformed-cursor guard at src/index.ts:141 plus the BUG-23 stale-cursor self-heal at :148-153); Redis has neither guard, and the shared conformance suite has no case for it.
failure: Input: `since = (Date.now()+3600000)+'-0'` on a topic that has messages, then keep posting. Reproduced: three consecutive `fetchRecent({topic, since: stale})` calls each returned `messages: []` with `nextCursor === stale` while 2, 3, 4 messages existed in the stream, and `fetchRecent({since: stale, blockMs: 1500})` blocked the whole budget and returned nothing. Wrong output: on-start catch-up returns nothing and stores the same dead cursor back, so the topic never catches up again (until wall-clock ms passes the stale value) and no error is ever raised. A malformed cursor ('abc', '', '$', '0-0-0') is no better: it throws the raw `ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument` with no backend/topic context, unlike sqlite's labelled message.
remediation: Mirror the sqlite contract: (1) validate `since` against `/^\d+(-\d+)?$/` and throw a labelled `parley-redis: malformed cursor '<x>' for topic <t>` otherwise; (2) compare `since` to `XINFO STREAM <key>` `lastGeneratedId` (or the last XREVRANGE id) and, when it is strictly greater, treat the call as `since === undefined` — return the default recent window and a live nextCursor — so catch-up self-heals after a dataset reset or a repointed instance_id.
testUpgrade: Add a shared conformance case, run against EVERY backend, parameterized over cursor provenance: [a cursor minted by this backend (must work), a syntactically-foreign cursor from another backend's format (must throw a labelled error), a well-formed cursor beyond this store's high-water mark (must self-heal to the default window, never an empty page echoing itself)]. Assert specifically `messages.length > 0 || nextCursor !== since` whenever the topic is non-empty — that single invariant catches the whole wedge class. Existing cases ('since at the tail', 'never-posted topic') only ever pass cursors this backend just minted, so they cannot see it.

summary: `retention_days` is taken verbatim from backend_config and multiplied into an XADD MINID threshold with no validation: `null` and `0` silently destroy history, a negative value deletes everything including the message just posted, and a large value produces a negative threshold that makes every post throw.
failure: Reproduced against live Redis. (a) `retention_days: null` — `null !== undefined` so trimming is ENABLED with threshold `Date.now() - 0 = now`: posted 260 messages, waited 1.5s, posted 10 more, `fetchRecent(limit:10000)` returned 81 messages starting at 'm179' — 179 messages silently deleted by a config value that reads as 'off' (and DESIGN §11 itself uses `null` to mean unset for `state_path`). (b) `retention_days: 0` behaves identically. (c) `retention_days: -1` — threshold is in the future, so fetchRecent returned `[]` and nextCursor '0-0' immediately after two successful posts: every post is deleted as it lands, forever, with no error. (d) `retention_days: 100000` — threshold goes negative and every `post` rejects with `ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument`, i.e. the bridge can never write again (the breakpoint is ~20663 days, so '99999 = keep forever' is a realistic spelling).
remediation: Validate in connect(): accept only a finite number > 0 whose `Date.now() - days*86_400_000` is >= 0; reject anything else with a loud error naming the key and the accepted range (`retention_days must be a positive number of days; omit it to keep every entry`). Treat `null` as omitted only if you also document it. Document in the README that there is no 'trim everything' mode.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'destructive numeric backend_config knobs must be validated, not coerced' with a table-driven test shared by every backend that owns its store (redis, sqlite, nats, postgres): for `retention_days` in [null, 0, -1, NaN, '7', 1e9, Infinity] assert either connect() rejects with a message naming the key, or (for the accepted values) that posting N messages and re-reading returns all N. bridge-redis currently has zero tests touching retention at all.

summary: The suite's reachability probe hardens the client exactly where the plugin does not (`connectTimeout: 800, reconnectStrategy: false`), which structurally guarantees no test can ever observe the plugin's forever-hang on connect; and the only white-box tests mock `redis` with a fake main client that has no xAdd/xRange/xRead, so the whole failure surface (connect failure, outage, retention, malformed/stale cursors) is untested by construction.
failure: Mutation that keeps the suite green: delete the fail-fast options from the plugin's client (they were never there) or add `socket: { reconnectStrategy: () => 1000 }` — every one of the 12 tests still passes, while `parley-redis` against a wrong URL hangs forever (verified). Same for making `retention_days` default to 0, or removing the `blockMs <= 0` floor in blockingRead: nothing in the package fails.

testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the test harness must not be more defensive than the code under test': add a lint/test assertion that any client options used by test probes are also used by the plugin (or, more durably, have the plugin export its `createClient` options builder and have the probe call it) — plus the parameterized backend-down and connect-failure suites named in the findings above, which are the coverage this file is currently missing.

summary: The README's two copy-paste commands publish an unauthenticated Redis on every interface (`docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine`, which also bypasses host firewalls), and the package documents no password, no `rediss://` TLS, and no `.env`/secret handling — despite CLAUDE.md ('secrets live in backend_config / .env, document secret handling in the README') and DESIGN §14 ('keep backends private'). bridge-postgres's README does carry the secrets note; this one does not.
failure: A self-hoster following DESIGN §10 (remote/chat mode requires an internet-reachable host) and this README ends up with port 6379 open to the internet with no AUTH: anyone can XRANGE every topic's full message history (agent context, handoffs), XADD forged messages as any `sender` — which core turns into `<channel>` events fed to a live Claude Code session (DESIGN §14 'inbound is untrusted', but the handle is spoofed) — and use the classic CONFIG SET dir/dbfilename write primitive.
remediation: Change the recipe to `docker run -d --name parley-redis -p 127.0.0.1:6379:6379 redis:7-alpine redis-server --requirepass "$REDIS_PASSWORD"`, and add a short 'Credentials & exposure' section: put the password in the URL via an env-sourced config (`url: redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@host:6379`), never commit it, use `rediss://` when the server is not on localhost, and never publish 6379 publicly.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'shipped infra recipes must not be insecure by default' with a repo-level docs test that scans every packages/*/README.md for `docker run` lines and fails any `-p <port>:<port>` that is not bound to 127.0.0.1 or not accompanied by an auth flag, and asserts each network-backend README contains a secrets/credentials section (the same check would have caught nats' `-p 4222:4222` line).

summary: connect() bumps the generation and overwrites `this.client` without disconnecting the previous client or tearing down the readers it superseded, so a reconnect leaks one live TCP connection per call (and leaves dead readers registered until the next disconnect).
failure: Reproduced with CLIENT LIST: connect + subscribe = +2 connections; a second connect() (no disconnect between) = +3; after `disconnect()` the count settles at +1 — one orphaned connection to Redis that is never closed for the life of the process. The class doc explicitly advertises the generation token as making 'disconnect()/reconnect' safe, so a caller is invited to do exactly this; a supervisor that reconnects on a persistent failure would leak a connection per attempt until Redis hits maxclients.
remediation: Make connect() idempotent/reentrant: at the top, if `this.client !== undefined` run the same teardown disconnect() does (bump generation, splice+disconnect all readers, disconnect the old client) before creating the new one — or throw a fail-fast 'already connected; call disconnect() first' so the contract is explicit rather than a silent leak.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'repeated lifecycle calls must not leak backend resources' with a parameterized lifecycle test run against every backend that holds sockets: for each sequence in [connect·connect·disconnect, connect·subscribe·connect·disconnect, connect·disconnect·disconnect, connect·subscribe·disconnect·connect·subscribe·disconnect], assert an externally observable resource count (Redis CLIENT LIST / NATS connz / open handles) returns to baseline. The existing BUG-37 tests assert only the in-process `readers` array, which stays clean here.

summary: subscribe() distinguishes 'stream does not exist yet' from a real failure by regex-matching the error text `/no such key/i`. Any server or proxy that words the missing-key error differently makes subscribe() throw instead of seeding lastId='0'.
failure: Input: subscribe to a topic whose stream has never been posted to, on a Redis-compatible endpoint whose XINFO STREAM error string differs (Valkey/ElastiCache/Upstash/a proxy that rewrites errors, or a future Redis rewording). Wrong output: subscribe() rejects, startPushLoop throws, and `bridge.attach()` fails — live push never starts for the entire session, and the failure looks like an infrastructure error rather than 'this topic is empty'. The inverse is worse but rarer: any unrelated error whose text happens to contain 'no such key' seeds lastId='0' and replays the whole retained history as <channel> push (the BUG-11 flood this code exists to prevent).
remediation: Classify structurally instead of textually: `const exists = await reader.exists(key); if (exists === 0) lastId = '0'; else lastId = (await reader.xInfoStream(key)).lastGeneratedId;` (or check `err instanceof ErrorReply` combined with an EXISTS re-probe) so the decision rests on server state, not on a human-readable string.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'branching on error message text' with a parameterized test that feeds the missing-stream path several plausible wordings — ['ERR no such key', 'ERR No such key.', 'NOKEY stream does not exist', 'ERR The stream specified does not exist'] — and asserts every one seeds lastId='0' and starts the loop, while ['LOADING …', 'READONLY …', 'NOPERM …'] all reject. A repo-wide grep test forbidding `/\btest\(String\(err/`-style message matching in plugins would keep the class from reappearing in the next backend.

summary: bridge-redis depends on `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` solely for a one-line `delay`, while that package's npm-published description states it is 'shared by the HTTP chat backends' and exists to keep 'SQLite/Redis/NATS/Postgres' free of HTTP concerns — the dependency graph now contradicts the metadata both packages ship to npm.
failure: Read the claim then the code: `packages/bridge-net-util/package.json` description says 'shared by the HTTP chat backends… NOT bridge-core: keeps the seam HTTP-free for SQLite/Redis/NATS/Postgres', and `src/index.ts:1-9` repeats it in JSDoc; yet `packages/bridge-redis/package.json:45` and `packages/bridge-postgres/package.json:45` list it as a runtime dependency, and bridge-redis's only use is `delay(100)` at src/index.ts:257. A user reading the npm page for parley-net-util is told the Redis plugin does not depend on it.
remediation: Either move the 3-line `delay` into `@sharptrick/parley-core` (it is transport-agnostic, not HTTP) and drop the net-util dependency from the non-HTTP plugins, or reword net-util's description/JSDoc to 'HTTP retry helper plus a shared sleep, used by the HTTP backends and by any plugin needing a delay'. Prefer the former: it removes a runtime dependency from the Redis tarball.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'shipped npm metadata must match the dependency graph' with a metadata test that parses each package.json description/keywords for package names and backend names it claims to relate to, and cross-checks them against the actual dependency lists — e.g. fail if a description enumerates packages as non-consumers while they appear in `dependencies`. Same test should assert every declared dependency is actually imported by that package's src.

summary: `recentWindow` (the no-`since` default window AND the BUG-10 expired-cursor fallback) asks the server for `limit` RAW timeline events and only then filters by topic/type — the exact defect BUG-03 fixed on the `since` path, left unfixed here. A topic whose messages sit behind `limit` foreign or non-`m.room.message` events returns an EMPTY page and cursor `''`, i.e. it is indistinguishable from a topic that has never been written to.
failure: Live Synapse, shared_room mode: post 3 messages to topic X, then 10 to topic Y in the same room, then `fetchRecent({ topic: X, limit: 5 })`. Expected `['x1','x2','x3']`; actual `[]` with `nextCursor === ''`. Same shape in the default per-topic-room mode whenever ≥`limit` reactions/edits/membership events sit at the tail. Combined with the sibling finding on the `''` cursor, topic X then stays invisible on every subsequent catch-up.
remediation: Give `recentWindow` the same drain loop `fetchSince` already has: page backwards (`dir=b`, `from=end`) up to MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES until `limit` BELONGING messages are collected or the timeline ends, then reverse to ascending. Do not let a raw page cap decide the result set.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven `fake.test.ts` case parameterized over (mode: shared_room | per-topic) x (noise: foreign-topic message | m.reaction | m.room.member) x (noiseCount: limit-1, limit, 3*limit), asserting that `fetchRecent({topic, limit})` returns ALL of the topic's messages regardless of noise depth. The same generator must also drive the BUG-10 fallback (a 404-ing `since`). Widen the shared conformance suite's `topics are isolated` case to post N > default-limit messages into a second topic before reading the first — as written it posts one message each and structurally cannot fail.

summary: An empty page yields `nextCursor = asCursor('')`. That value is persisted to read-state, and replaying it hits `GET /rooms/<id>/context/?limit=0`, which Synapse answers `404 M_NOT_FOUND` (verified by curl) — so the BUG-10 'expired cursor' fallback fires and resumes from the most-recent-`limit` window, silently discarding every message older than it. A sentinel meaning 'beginning of stream' is being decoded as 'cursor expired'.
failure: Live Synapse: `fetchRecent({topic: T})` on a never-posted topic → `nextCursor === ''`; persist it; post m1..m5; `catchUpTopic({plugin, topic: T, limit: 3, readState, seen})` returns 3, not 5 — m1 and m2 are never delivered and the persisted cursor jumps past them. With the default `catchup.limit: 100`, any topic that accumulates >100 messages between the first (empty) catch-up and the next one loses the overflow permanently.
remediation: Do not mint `''`. Either (a) return the room's current backward pagination token as the cursor for an empty window and teach `fetchSince` to accept a `/messages` token as well as an event id, or (b) mint an explicit sentinel (e.g. `'@start'`) that `fetchSince` maps to 'page forward from the beginning of the visible timeline' rather than to the recent-window fallback. Reserve the 404 fallback for cursors that are genuinely non-empty and unresolvable.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a cursor this backend minted must, when replayed, return exactly the messages after it — never a truncated window'. Add a parameterized round-trip test over cursors minted from {empty topic, single-message topic, topic whose window was all-foreign, purged event id} x {0, limit-1, limit, 3*limit messages posted afterwards}, asserting `catchUpTopic` drains ALL posted messages. Promote the same generator into packages/conformance so every backend is held to it; today `fetchRecent on a never-posted topic returns an empty page with a replayable cursor` replays the cursor with ZERO intervening posts, so it cannot catch this.

summary: `resolveOrCreateRoom` creates every topic room with `preset: 'public_chat'`. Verified against live Synapse: the resulting room has `join_rule: public` and `history_visibility: shared`. `visibility: 'private'` only hides it from the room directory — it does not restrict joins. The alias is deterministic (`#parley_<sanitizedTopic>:<server_name>`), so it is guessable, and Synapse federates by default.
failure: Any account on the homeserver (or, with federation on, any account anywhere that guesses/learns `#parley_ctx-payments:parley.local`) can `POST /join` uninvited, read the entire Parley history for that topic, and post messages that core delivers into a live Claude Code session as `<channel>` events — the prompt-injection surface DESIGN §14 says to minimize by 'locking write access to known handles'. Posting into the `parley-presence` room the same way injects arbitrary peers into every bridge's `parley_list_users` roster.
remediation: Default to an invite-only room: `preset: 'private_chat'` (or explicit `initial_state` with `m.room.join_rules: invite` and `m.room.history_visibility: invited`), and expose an opt-in `room_preset`/`invite` knob in `backend_config` for deployments that deliberately want a human-joinable room. Document the change in the README seam table, which currently advertises `preset: public_chat` with no security note.
testUpgrade: Class = 'rooms/channels this plugin provisions must not be world-readable/world-writable by default'. Add a fake-Synapse test that captures the `POST /createRoom` body for every provisioning path (first post, first fetch, first subscribe, presence topic) and asserts the join rule is not `public` — parameterized over shared_room on/off and over a config that opts back in, so the opt-in stays deliberate. Pair it with a live-homeserver test (skipped when Synapse is absent) that reads `m.room.join_rules` back off the created room, so a preset that silently changes server-side is caught too.

summary: `liveRooms` is keyed by room_id but `wakeRoomWaiters` only wakes waiters whose `topic` matches the topic the subscribe loop just delivered. In shared_room mode every topic maps to ONE room, so a `subscribe(A)` anywhere in the process makes `blockingFetch` on topic B skip its dedicated `/sync` ('a loop already covers this room') while that loop will never wake a B waiter. The waiter's only remaining wake source is the `blockMs` timeout.
failure: Live Synapse, shared_room mode: `subscribe(A, noop)`; seed topic B; `fetchRecent({topic: B, since: tail, blockMs: 4000})`; post to B at t=200ms. Measured return at 4028ms (the full budget) instead of ~200ms — reproduced. In production `catchup.block_max_ms` defaults to 60000, so an agent long-polling topic B waits up to 60s for a message that already landed. Same shape (narrower window) in per-topic mode: `subscribe` adds the room to `liveRooms` BEFORE it awaits its `timeout=0` positioning sync, so a message landing during that window is skipped by the loop's positioning and the waiter that trusted the loop idles out its budget.
remediation: Scope the live-coverage flag by (room_id, topic) rather than room_id — a blocking fetch may only hook a subscribe loop that actually delivers ITS topic — and register that flag only after the loop's positioning sync has resolved (or, simpler, always drive the dedicated bounded `/sync`; it is cheap and removes the coupling entirely).
testUpgrade: Class = 'a parked long-poll must be woken by whatever actually observes its message, or drive its own observer'. Add a parameterized fake-Synapse matrix over (shared_room on/off) x (subscribed topic == blocked topic | != blocked topic | no subscribe at all) x (subscribe started before / concurrently with the blocking fetch), asserting every cell returns within a small fraction of `blockMs`. The existing `issue #20` tests only cover the no-subscribe case, so none of them can fire.

summary: The shared suite posts with `SENDER = asHandle('writer')` in every case but never asserts anything about `Message.senderHandle`. Matrix drops the seam's `identity` argument entirely (`void identity`) and reports the homeserver-stamped MXID instead, so DESIGN §5's 'senderHandle: logical sender' is not what crosses the seam — and nothing in the suite would notice if any backend regressed the same way.
failure: Mutation test: delete the `sender` mapping in a backend and hardcode `sender: 'anon'` — the whole conformance suite stays green. Concretely on Matrix, `computeRoster` keys on `m.senderHandle` (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts:202), so `parley_list_users` lists `@parley:parley.local` rather than the configured `identity.handle`, and two sessions sharing the default account collapse into one roster handle.
remediation: Add a `senderHandle` assertion to the conformance suite behind a context flag that says how the backend derives it (`identityIsLogical: true` for sqlite/redis/nats/postgres, an explicit mapper for the chat backends), so 'this backend substitutes a backend identity' is a declared, reviewed property rather than an untested silence. For Matrix specifically, consider carrying the logical handle in the event content next to `app.parley.topic` and preferring it on read (falling back to `sender`), since it already writes a custom content key.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the suite's post→fetchRecent and live-push cases over a `expectSender(handle)` hook supplied by each backend factory, defaulting to strict equality with the posted handle; backends that legitimately stamp their own identity must supply an explicit mapper, which makes the deviation visible in the factory rather than invisible in the assertions.

summary: The `subscribe` `/sync` loop catches every error with an empty handler, waits a fixed 200ms, and continues forever. There is no logging, no backoff escalation, and no re-authentication path — a permanent failure (an invalidated access token → `401 M_UNKNOWN_TOKEN`, a room the account was kicked from → 403) turns the live-push path into an invisible 5 Hz hammer on the homeserver.
failure: Invalidate the bridge's device token (Synapse `POST /logout` from another client) while a bridge is subscribed. `http()` throws on 401 (not in `allowStatuses`), the catch swallows it, and the loop re-issues `/sync` every 200ms indefinitely. Live push is dead; stderr stays empty; the operator's only symptom is homeserver load. `connect()` is never retried, so the process never recovers on its own.
remediation: Log the failure to stderr (rate-limited, e.g. first occurrence plus every Nth), apply exponential backoff with a cap instead of a flat 200ms, and on a 401/`M_UNKNOWN_TOKEN` re-run the `m.login.password` step once before giving up (or surface a fatal so the supervisor restarts the bridge).
testUpgrade: Class = 'a background loop must not turn a permanent error into a silent infinite retry'. Fake-Synapse test parameterized over the failure the server returns to `/sync` ({401, 403, 500, network reject}) x {transient (fails 3x then recovers), permanent}: assert the transient cases recover and deliver, and that the permanent cases (a) emit at least one stderr diagnostic and (b) issue fewer than K requests in a fixed wall-clock window (proving backoff). Apply the same table to the other backends' subscribe loops.

summary: `post` accepts `_opts?: { inReplyTo }` and discards it with no comment, no README line, and no error. Core exposes `in_reply_to` on both `parley_post` and `parley_reply` ('Optional backendMsgId this message threads under'), and Matrix is the backend that supports threading most natively (`m.relates_to` / `m.in_reply_to`). The README's `post` row documents the sent content exactly and omits any mention of threading, so the tool's documented promise is silently unmet here. bridge-zulip, by contrast, documents its own ignore in a JSDoc line.
failure: `parley_post({topic: 't', content: 'ack', in_reply_to: '$abc:server'})` against Matrix returns a fresh `backendMsgId` and the message lands with no relation; a human in Element sees an unthreaded message, and a later reader cannot recover the thread. No warning is emitted anywhere.
remediation: Populate `m.relates_to: { 'm.in_reply_to': { event_id: inReplyTo } }` when `opts.inReplyTo` is supplied (a two-line change to the send body); if that is deliberately out of scope, say so in a JSDoc line on `post` and in the README seam table, as bridge-zulip does.
testUpgrade: Class = 'every seam argument is either honored or documented as ignored'. Add a repo-wide table-driven test that, for each plugin, posts with `inReplyTo` and asserts either the backend record carries the relation OR the plugin's `post` JSDoc contains an explicit 'inReplyTo is ignored' clause — so a future backend cannot join the silent-drop group by accident. Extend it to `identity` for the same reason.

summary: The long-poll waiter is armed only after the initial exclusive MAM query has already returned empty, and nothing re-checks the archive once it is armed, so a message reflected during that query round trip is never woken on and the fetch idles out the entire blockMs budget.
failure: Live probe against Prosody: post 'old', take the tail cursor, call fetchRecent({since: tail, blockMs: 5000}) with a 400 ms latency injected into the first exclusiveMam (a realistic remote round trip), then post 'fresh' at t=100 ms. Expected prompt return (~150 ms, as the conformance case asserts for the fast path); actual return at 5410 ms with the message — the full budget burned. Core's blocking-fetch wrapper cannot rescue it because the plugin consumed the whole remaining budget in one call, so the MCP caller waits up to catchup.block_max_ms (60 s) for a message that arrived 100 ms in.
remediation: Adopt the shape already used in packages/bridge-matrix/src/index.ts blockingFetch: register the room waiter FIRST (bounded by the remaining budget), then run the exclusive MAM query; if that re-check returns rows, cancel the waiter and return immediately; only then park on `fired`. Loop on the remaining budget so a spurious wake re-arms rather than returning early.
testUpgrade: Class = lost wakeup from arming the wake source after the state snapshot. Add a parameterized long-poll test (shared, table-driven across every natively-blocking backend, driven from packages/conformance) that injects a delay at each stage of the blocking path — before the first query, between query and arm, between arm and park — and posts a message inside each injected window, asserting the fetch returns within a small multiple of the injected delay rather than at the deadline. The existing conformance 'blockMs long-poll' case posts at a fixed 50 ms against a sub-millisecond local query, so its window is never hit; it only asserts >=150 ms elapsed, never an upper bound on latency.

summary: pendingJoins is keyed by room only and joinOnce overwrites the previous entry without cancelling its 15 s timer; when a reconnect fires a re-join while a join is still in flight, the stale timer deletes the successor's entry, so the re-join's self-presence is dropped and live push for that room never resumes.
failure: Fake-client probe: subscribe(t1) leaves a pending join, then emit 'online' twice (the reconnect path clears `joined` and calls ensureJoined again, registering a second PendingJoin under the same room key). Advance 15 s: the FIRST join's timer runs `pendingJoins.delete(room)` and deletes the NEW entry (map size 1 -> 0). Feeding the room's self-presence (status code 110) is then ignored by onPresence (no pending entry), so the re-join stays unresolved until its own 15 s timeout rejects — and that rejection is swallowed by `void this.ensureJoined(...).catch(() => undefined)` in the online handler. Net effect: after a reconnect that races an in-flight join, the bridge is silently no longer a MUC occupant, subscribe() delivers nothing and every subsequent post() times out at 15 s.
remediation: Make the pending-join slot own its lifecycle: on registering a new PendingJoin for a room, reject/clear any existing one first; have each entry's timer/reject path delete only itself (`if (this.pendingJoins.get(room) === entry) this.pendingJoins.delete(room)`), the same identity guard ensureJoined already uses for the `joined` cache. Also surface the swallowed re-join failure (stderr) and retry it instead of dropping it.
testUpgrade: Class = timer/callback registered in a single-slot map deleting or resolving a successor's registration. Add a table-driven test over the plugin's keyed pending maps (pendingJoins, pendingPosts, mamCollectors, waiters) that, for each, registers entry A, replaces/re-registers for the same key as B, fires A's timeout, and asserts B is still registered and still completes on its own event; run it with vi.useFakeTimers so the 15 s path is cheap. The existing reconnect-rejoin.test.ts only asserts a presence was re-sent and never advances timers past JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS.

summary: onStanza drops every `<message type='error'>`, so a MUC rejection of a post (not an occupant, no voice in a moderated room, kicked/banned, room destroyed) is never correlated to the in-flight post; the call hangs the full 15 s POST_TIMEOUT_MS and then rejects with a generic message that hides the server's condition.
failure: Live probe: pre-seed the join cache for a room and call post(topic, handle, 'hello'). Prosody answers `<message type='error'>` with not-acceptable immediately, but onStanza's `if (stanza.attrs.type !== 'groupchat') return` discards it; the promise rejected only after 15008 ms with 'post reflection timeout in p-zwdgtc@muc.parley.local'. The same 15 s stall per post occurs for any real revocation (voice removed in a moderated room, occupancy lost after a MUC service restart that does not drop the stream) and the operator/agent gets no cause.
remediation: Handle `type === 'error'` in onStanza: extract `<origin-id>`/`id` and, when it matches a pendingPost, reject it immediately with the XMPP error condition and text; when it matches a room with a pending join, reject that too. Include the condition in the thrown Error so the MCP caller sees 'forbidden'/'not-acceptable' rather than a timeout.
testUpgrade: Class = a protocol error response that the stanza router silently discards, converting a fast failure into a timeout. Add a parameterized test feeding onStanza a table of realistic error stanzas — message type='error' with each of not-acceptable / forbidden / item-not-found / gone, and presence type='error' with conflict / registration-required / service-unavailable — and assert in every row that the correlated post/join promise rejects promptly with the condition string in the message, and that no timer is left armed. No current test feeds any error stanza.

summary: onGroupchat resolves a pending post from ANY occupant's message that carries a matching `<origin-id>`, with no check that the reflection came from our own occupant JID — the exact provenance check SEC-13 added for MAM results was never applied to the post correlator, and the correlator itself is Math.random-derived.
failure: Injected the stanza a server would deliver for another occupant's message that copies our origin-id — `<message from='room@muc/attacker' type='groupchat'><body/><origin-id id='o-predicted'/><stanza-id by='room@muc' id='ATTACKER-ARCHIVE-ID'/></message>` — into onStanza while an in-flight post awaited 'o-predicted'. post() resolved with 'ATTACKER-ARCHIVE-ID', i.e. the caller's own message is recorded (and dedup-keyed/cursored) at another occupant's archive position. Origin-ids are `o-` + two Math.random base36 tokens and are published in the room on every post, so a co-occupant can recover the v8 PRNG state from observed outputs and pre-send the next id; only the send/reflect race remains, and it can be flooded.
remediation: Before resolving a pendingPost, require `resourceOf(stanza.attrs.from) === this.nick` (a MUC reflection of our own message always comes from our own occupant JID) and that bareOf(from) equals the room we posted to. Mint origin-id (and the default nick suffix) with crypto.randomUUID()/randomBytes rather than Math.random, matching the queryid fix.
testUpgrade: Class = a correlator matched on an attacker-visible token without verifying the stanza's sender. Add a parameterized 'foreign-provenance' suite that, for each correlated id in the plugin (origin-id -> pendingPosts, queryid -> mamCollectors, room -> pendingJoins/waiters/subscriptions), feeds a well-formed stanza bearing the right token but a wrong `from` (other occupant, other room, other bare JID, missing from) and asserts nothing is resolved or collected — plus the mutation-guard negative control the MAM test already uses. Also assert every generated correlator matches the crypto-UUID/hex shape, not a Math.random token.

summary: The README (and examples/multi-session/xmpp/code-agent-a.yaml) promise that copying a pinned `nick` into a second concurrent session 'fails outright — a loud error, not a silent split'; with the shared account the same docs recommend, both sessions join happily and every message is attributed to the same nick.
failure: Live probe: two XmppPlugin instances, both connect({username:'parley', password:'parleypass', nick:'fixed-nick'}), both subscribe and post to one topic. No error at any point. Archive reads back 'fixed-nick:from-a | fixed-nick:from-b' and session A's live handler sees both under the same sender — exactly the silent split the README says cannot happen here (XEP-0045 permits the same bare JID to occupy a room under one nick from multiple resources). An operator following the README will treat pinning a nick as safe-because-it-would-have-crashed and get silently merged senders across sessions.
remediation: Correct the README's 'Multiple concurrent sessions' bullet and the code-agent-a.yaml comment: a duplicate pinned nick is only a loud `conflict` error when the sessions use DIFFERENT accounts; with the shared account the docs recommend it silently merges sender identity. Optionally make the plugin defend — append a per-connection suffix to a configured nick, or refuse to start when a pinned nick is combined with a shared username.
testUpgrade: Class = a README safety claim of the form 'this misconfiguration fails loudly' that no test exercises. Add a table-driven multi-session test (one row per divergence the README lists: shared account + pinned nick, differing muc_service, differing domain) that stands up two plugins with that config pair and asserts the documented outcome — error thrown, or distinct senders — so any doc claim of a loud failure is mechanically pinned to observed behaviour.

summary: An unknown/expired `since` (RSM `<after>` UID no longer in the archive) is not detected: this Prosody ignores the unknown `<after>` and returns the archive from the beginning, so exclusive-since silently degrades to a full replay — contradicting both the in-code comment that servers reply item-not-found and the README's retention claim that pruning just returns less history.
failure: Live probe: post 'a' to a fresh topic, then fetchRecent({since: asCursor('deadbeef-not-in-archive')}). Expected either an error or an empty page; actual: resolved with 1 message (the entire archive) and a cursor pointing at it. With MAM's archive_expires_after (Prosody default '1w'), a bridge resuming on a cursor older than the window re-delivers the whole surviving archive instead of the promised 'less history'; core's backendMsgId dedup hides the duplicates but the exclusive-since guarantee and the fetch cost are both violated.
remediation: Either detect the condition (compare the first returned archId against `since` provenance, or issue a bounded `<before>`-anchored probe for the cursor before paging) and surface it as a resume-from-start with a stderr warning, or fix the two documents: change the comment at src/index.ts:556 to say the behaviour is server-dependent, and change the README retention paragraph to say an expired cursor can replay the surviving archive rather than returning less history.
testUpgrade: Class = the plugin's assumption about a server's response to an out-of-range/unknown cursor going untested. Add a parameterized catch-up test over cursor inputs — '' , a valid cursor, a syntactically valid but unknown id, a cursor from a different room, a very long/garbage string — asserting for each that the call either resolves with a documented behaviour or rejects with a typed error, and that the resulting nextCursor is replayable. No current test passes a cursor the archive does not contain.

summary: Every non-conformance test in this package hand-feeds a well-formed stanza to private state on the happy path; nothing injects latency, an error stanza, a presence error, a failing MAM IQ, or a mid-operation disconnect, which is why three of the confirmed defects above (wake gap, join aliasing, error-stanza stall) sit under a fully green suite.
failure: Mutation check: delete the `fireWaiters(room)` call in onGroupchat and the suite still passes locally (the blockMs conformance case only requires the fetch to return the message and to have waited >=150 ms — with the deadline re-query it still does). Likewise, making joinOnce's timeout delete an unrelated key, or dropping error stanzas, changes no assertion. The suite therefore cannot distinguish 'wakes promptly' from 'times out and re-queries'.
remediation: Add a fault-injection harness for this plugin: a scriptable fake XmppClient (send/iqCaller/stanza pump) that can inject configurable latency per IQ, emit error stanzas and presence errors, drop occupancy, and fire 'online' at arbitrary points — then drive the plugin's public API through it. Give the conformance blockMs case an upper-bound latency assertion in addition to the lower bound.
testUpgrade: Class = a suite that only exercises success paths, so failure-path regressions are invisible. Parameterize a fault matrix (stage of the operation x fault kind: latency, error stanza, IQ rejection, disconnect, reconnect-online) and assert the invariant for each cell — bounded latency, prompt typed rejection, no leaked timers/map entries (assert pendingJoins/pendingPosts/mamCollectors/waiters are all empty after each case).

summary: Stream errors are swallowed by `xmpp.on('error', () => undefined)` with no stderr diagnostic, and a non-retryable MUC join error is reported with its condition flattened to the literal 'error', so an operator debugging a flapping stream or a rejected join has nothing to go on.
failure: Trace: onPresence computes `RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS.find(c => errEl?.getChild(c) !== undefined) ?? 'error'`, so a `conflict`, `forbidden`, `registration-required`, `not-authorized` or `service-unavailable` (room full) presence error all surface identically as 'MUC join error (error) for room@muc.parley.local'. Combined with the silent 'error' handler, a bridge that is auth-flapping or banned from a room prints nothing to stderr and every post fails with an indistinguishable message. (Also: `@xmpp/debug` is declared as a runtime dependency and imported nowhere — it ships to npm consumers as dead weight and extra supply-chain surface.)
remediation: Log stream errors to stderr (never stdout — cli.ts is a JSON-RPC channel) with rate limiting; parse the actual XMPP error condition from `<error>`'s child element regardless of whether it is retryable and put it, plus any `<text>`, in the JoinError message; move `@xmpp/debug` to devDependencies or drop it.
testUpgrade: Class = diagnostics discarded on the failure path. Add a parameterized test over presence/message error conditions (retryable and non-retryable alike) asserting the thrown Error message contains the exact condition token, plus a test that an emitted stream 'error' produces a stderr write and never a stdout write; and add a repo-level check (extend the existing publish preflight) that every declared runtime dependency is actually imported by the package's src.

summary: connect() takes nats.js's default reconnect policy (10 attempts / 2s) and nothing watches nc.closed(), so any outage longer than ~20s permanently bricks the plugin — silently for subscribe, and forever for post/fetchRecent.
failure: Repro (scratch script, TCP proxy in front of a real JetStream server): subscribe to topic `part`, receive 'before', then blackhole the socket for 35s and heal it. After healing: 'during' and 'after' are never delivered (the subscribe loop exited because `recreate` was false, no rebuild), and `sub.fetchRecent({topic})` / `sub.post(...)` both throw `CONNECTION_CLOSED` on every subsequent call for the life of the process. No error is surfaced on the live path at all — the bridge just goes deaf.
remediation: Pass `maxReconnectAttempts: -1` (plus a bounded `reconnectTimeWait`/jitter) to `connect()`, and additionally register a watcher on `nc.closed()` / `nc.status()` that re-runs the connect+resubscribe path (recreating consumers at `lastSeq + 1` per topic) instead of leaving `stopped === false` with a dead connection. Failing that, at minimum fail loudly: surface the closed connection so core reports it rather than silently ceasing delivery.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a network-fault table over outage duration and fault kind — {socket reset, blackhole 5s, blackhole 35s (> default reconnect budget), server restart} x {post, fetchRecent, subscribe} — driven by an in-test TCP proxy fixture, asserting for each cell that after the fault heals a post is (a) delivered live and (b) visible via catch-up from the pre-fault cursor. reconnect.test.ts today only deletes a consumer while the connection is healthy, so it cannot reach this class; the proxy fixture belongs next to it (and is reusable by every socket backend).

summary: When the no-`since` catch-up read yields zero messages (fetch expiry of 2000ms, slow link, filter mismatch) fetchRecent returns nextCursor = lastSeq, jumping the persisted read position to the tail past messages it never returned — silent, permanent message loss.
failure: Repro (scratch script): 3 messages posted to a topic; a proxy delays every server->client byte by 2.6s (> the hardcoded `expires: 2000`). `fetchRecent({topic})` returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '3' }` with no error. Core persists cursor 3; the follow-up `fetchRecent({topic, since:'3'})` returns [] — 'a','b','c' are lost forever. Same code path reproduced deterministically with a subject_prefix mismatch (filter matches nothing): [] with nextCursor '1' while seq 1 was never read.
remediation: Never fabricate `lastSeq` as the cursor for a page you did not read. In the non-empty branch, when `messages.length === 0` return `asCursor(String(startSeq - 1))` (resume immediately before the unread window); better, treat `messages.length < want` after the fetch iterator ends early as a partial/failed read and either return the last-read cursor only or throw so core retries. Also make the 2000ms fetch expiry proportional to the work (or retry) rather than a fixed constant.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a page that returned fewer messages than the window contained must not advance the cursor past them'. Add a table-driven case over {no-since first catch-up, since-based catch-up, blockMs long-poll} x {read complete, read partial, read empty} using a latency/fault-injecting transport fixture, asserting the invariant: after any fetchRecent, replaying the returned nextCursor as `since` must still yield every message that was not in `messages`. Existing conformance cases only exercise the happy path, where the returned page is always complete.

summary: rowToMessage trusts the JSON.parse result: a payload of `null` or one whose `content` is not a string throws out of fetchRecent, and since the message stays in the stream forever, catch-up for that topic is permanently dead — a one-publish denial of service from any client with publish rights on the subject.
failure: Repro (scratch script, real server): publish the raw bytes `null` to `<subject_prefix><topic>` (any NATS client can), then `fetchRecent({topic})` -> throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'sender')`. Publish `{"content":123}` -> `TypeError: content.matchAll is not a function`. Every subsequent catch-up covering that sequence throws identically; the agent never receives another message on that topic. On the live path the throw is swallowed by the best-effort handler catch, so the message vanishes with no diagnostic at all.
remediation: Validate the decoded frame before building a Message: require a non-null plain object and coerce/reject non-string fields (`typeof x === 'string' ? x : ''`, or skip the record entirely). Wrap the whole per-record decode in try/catch inside the fetch loop so one malformed record is dropped (and logged to stderr) rather than failing the page. CLAUDE.md's 'inbound is untrusted' applies to the wire format, not just the content.
testUpgrade: Class = 'no byte sequence on the topic subject may throw out of fetchRecent or subscribe'. Add a fuzz/table case publishing raw payloads out of a generator — `null`, `[]`, `"str"`, `123`, `{}`, `{content:<non-string>}`, `{sender:<object>}`, truncated JSON, invalid UTF-8, 1MB of NULs — and assert fetchRecent resolves, returns a Message per record, and every field is a string. Ideally hoist it into the shared conformance suite as an optional `injectRawRecord(topic, bytes)` hook so every JSON-payload backend is covered.

summary: The BUG-02 test's stated contract — rebuild at DeliverPolicy.StartSequence lastSeq+1 'so the outage gap is backfilled' — is not asserted: it posts only after the loss, so deleting the entire backfill logic leaves the suite green.
failure: Mutation run: replaced `deliver_policy: lastSeq === undefined ? DeliverPolicy.New : DeliverPolicy.StartSequence, ...(opt_start_seq: lastSeq+1)` with an unconditional `DeliverPolicy.New` and ran `npx vitest run packages/bridge-nats/test/reconnect.test.ts` -> 2/2 passed. The regression the test exists to prevent (messages published during the consumer outage are dropped) is invisible to it. Source restored; `git diff` empty.
remediation: Publish the gap message while the consumer is absent — delete the consumer, post 'during-gap', wait past the plugin's rebuild backoff, then assert `got` contains 'during-gap' in order before 'after'. Deleting the consumer via jsm and immediately posting is too fast on localhost, so add a controllable delay (proxy pause, or an injectable rebuild backoff) to widen the outage window deterministically.
testUpgrade: Class = 'recovery tests must assert the gap is backfilled, not merely that delivery resumes'. Parameterize over outage cause {consumer deleted, stream consumer GC'd, connection dropped} x {message delivered before the outage, no message delivered before the outage} and assert the full expected sequence including messages published *during* the outage. Run the suite under a mutation check (invert deliver_policy / drop opt_start_seq) in CI or as a documented manual gate, since these tests currently pass against a plugin with no backfill at all.

summary: Non-string values from an untrusted publisher pass unchecked through buildMessage into Message.senderHandle and Message.timestamp, so a value that is typed `string` above the seam is actually an arbitrary JSON object at runtime.
failure: Repro: publishing `{"sender":{"x":1},"content":"hi"}` yields a Message whose `senderHandle` is the object `{x:1}`; `{"content":"ok","ts":{"a":1}}` yields `timestamp` = `{a:1}`. Both are delivered on the live path and via catch-up, and flow into core's identity/mention filtering and the MCP tool output, where any `.toLowerCase()`/glob match on a handle will throw or mismatch — an attacker-controlled type confusion across the seam.
remediation: Coerce defensively in rowToMessage: `typeof fields.sender === 'string' ? fields.sender : ''` for sender/content/ts (or drop records that fail validation). The seam's contract is that these are strings; the plugin is the boundary that must make that true.
testUpgrade: Same generator as the poison-payload upgrade, with the additional assertion `typeof m.senderHandle === 'string' && typeof m.content === 'string' && typeof m.timestamp === 'string'` for every Message returned by fetchRecent and passed to a subscribe handler — a property assertion over a generated payload space, not a fixed list.

summary: `ensured` memoizes a *successful* stream creation forever, so if the stream is removed out-of-band (admin `nats stream rm`, JetStream storage reset, a purge/recreate) the plugin never recreates it and every post/fetch fails until the process restarts.
failure: Repro: post to a topic (stream created), delete the stream with jsm.streams.delete, then `post` -> throws `503` (opaque no-responders) and `fetchRecent` -> throws `stream not found`; the ensured entry is a resolved promise, so ensureStream is a no-op on every retry and the topic stays broken for the process lifetime. BUG-01 fixed the cached-rejection half of this; the cached-success half is the mirror image.
remediation: Treat 'stream missing' as a cache invalidation: catch the 503 / stream-not-found from publish/consumers.add/streams.info, `this.ensured.delete(name)`, and retry ensureStream once before propagating. Optionally re-verify with streams.info on a TTL rather than memoizing unconditionally.
testUpgrade: Class = 'externally removed backend resources must be re-provisioned, not cached as present'. Table-driven: for each of {stream deleted, stream purged, consumer deleted, whole JetStream account reset}, assert that the next post and the next fetchRecent succeed (recreating what is missing) rather than throwing. recovery.test.ts covers only the rejection-caching half.

summary: When the consumer is lost before it has ever delivered a message, the rebuild uses DeliverPolicy.New — the comment's 'no gap to backfill yet' is false, since messages published during the outage are silently skipped.
failure: Traced: `lastSeq` is only assigned inside the message loop. Subscribe to a quiet topic, lose the consumer (server-side GC after 30s of client absence during a partition), have a peer post during the outage: on rebuild the consumer starts at New and those messages never reach the handler. Core's periodic catch-up may mask it, but the live-push contract is violated silently. Not reproduced on localhost — the rebuild completes within ~3ms of the delete, so the observable window closes before a post can land.
remediation: Seed `lastSeq` at subscribe time from `streams.info().state.last_seq` (the position at which DeliverPolicy.New effectively starts) so every rebuild — including the first — resumes at StartSequence lastSeq+1 and backfills the outage. Then delete the two-branch deliver_policy special case.
testUpgrade: Cover the 'never delivered before the loss' cell explicitly in the recovery table above (outage cause x whether a message was delivered pre-outage), with the outage widened by an injectable rebuild backoff or proxy pause so it is deterministic rather than a localhost timing accident.

summary: README and the npm `description` both advertise an 'ordered consumer' for live push, but the code deliberately uses a plain named ephemeral consumer — the source JSDoc even says so and explains that it does not self-heal.
failure: README table: "`subscribe` | a `consume()` ordered consumer with `DeliverPolicy.New`"; package.json:5 description: "an ordered consumer for live push" (this string ships to npm). src/index.ts:242 JSDoc: "A plain named ephemeral consumer is GC'd by the server ... and `consume()` does not self-heal". A reader who believes the README expects nats.js OrderedConsumer semantics (automatic gap detection and reset) and will not implement the recovery handling this plugin actually needs.
remediation: Change both strings to 'an ephemeral `consume()` consumer at DeliverPolicy.New with an explicit rebuild-on-loss watcher', or switch the implementation to a real ordered consumer. Note the README also claims the topic fold is just 'sanitized to `_`' and that the stream is `PARLEY_<topic>`, omitting safeName's `-<sha1>` disambiguation suffix — so `nats stream ls` will not show the documented name for any topic containing `.`, `*`, `>`, `/` or whitespace.
testUpgrade: Class = 'public claims must be mechanically tied to code'. Add a docs-conformance test that (a) asserts package.json description/keywords against a constant exported from src, and (b) for each README mapping-table row, asserts the corresponding behaviour — e.g. a test computing the stream/subject name for a table of topics ('plain', 'a.b', 'a/b', 'a b', unicode) and comparing it to the names the README documents.

summary: fetchRecent creates a server-side ephemeral consumer with no try/finally, so any throw from consumers.get/fetch leaks it — the exact hazard blockingFetch's comment says must be covered by a finally.
failure: If `consumers.get` or `consumer.fetch` rejects (connection blip, timeout) between lines 151-157, `consumers.delete` at line 158 is never reached and the consumer lingers until the 30s inactive_threshold. Under a flapping link with per-topic polling this accumulates consumers on the server; the code also never closes the `batch` iterator on the early `break`.
remediation: Wrap everything after `consumers.add` in try/finally exactly as blockingFetch does, closing `batch` and deleting the consumer in the finally. Better: eliminate the divergence by having both paths share one 'ephemeral consumer session' helper.
testUpgrade: Class = 'every server-side resource this plugin creates is destroyed on every exit path'. Table-driven over {fetchRecent, blockingFetch, subscribe} x {normal return, throw mid-read, disconnect mid-call}, asserting via jsm.consumers.list that the stream's consumer count returns to its pre-call value (allowing only the live subscribe consumer).

summary: NatsBackendConfig exposes no credentials or TLS options and connect() passes only `{ servers }`, so the documented deployment story is an unauthenticated NATS server — while DESIGN §14 promises 'NATS creds live in backend_config'.
failure: `await connect({ servers: cfg.servers ?? '127.0.0.1:4222' })` is the entire connection surface: no `authenticator` (creds file / nkey / JWT — the standard for any real or NGS deployment), no `token`, no `user`/`pass` field, no `tls` CA/cert options. A user with a secured cluster can only smuggle `user:pass` into the servers URL, which is undocumented, and cannot use a creds file at all. The README's only run instructions start an open, auth-free server.
remediation: Add explicit optional config: `token`, `user`/`pass`, `creds_file`/`nkey_seed` (wired to nats.js `credsAuthenticator`/`nkeyAuthenticator`, read from disk at connect), and `tls: { ca_file, cert_file, key_file }`; document them in the README as belonging in backend_config/.env and never in core. Ensure none of them are echoed in error messages or the CLI's stderr banner.
testUpgrade: Class = 'every backend_config field the docs promise is actually honoured, and secrets never leak'. Table-driven over the config keys: for each, assert it reaches the driver (spy on the mocked `connect`) and that the key's value never appears in any thrown error message or stderr output. Add an auth-enabled NATS service to examples/dev-compose so at least one credentialed connect is exercised for real in CI.

summary: subscribe() probes the gap-fill watermark AFTER registering the event queue, so any message that lands in that window is counted as already-delivered and is then permanently skipped by the event loop's `id <= lastDeliveredId` dedup — it reaches the handler zero times, not once.
failure: Reproduced with a scratch test that intercepts global fetch and posts 'racer' after `POST /api/v1/register` returns but before the tail probe `GET /api/v1/messages?...num_before=1` is served: `lastDeliveredId` becomes racer's id, the queue event for racer is dropped by the `<=` check, and the handler receives only the later 'after' — `expected [ 'after' ] to deeply equal [ 'racer', 'after' ]`. The inline comment on line 344-345 claims the opposite ("a message landing in between is never lost — worst case it is delivered once via the queue"), so the comment is also false.
remediation: Probe the tail BEFORE `register()` (then the worst case is a duplicate-free extra delivery via the queue, since any message arriving in the window has id > the baseline), or make the dedup exclusive of the baseline only for ids the loop itself delivered. Fix the comment to match whichever ordering is chosen.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'live-path watermark must never be seeded from state observed after the subscription tail'. Add a table-driven test that, for each injection point in the subscribe handshake (before register, between register and the tail probe, between the tail probe and the first /events poll, and between two /events polls), posts a message via a fetch interceptor/fake hook and asserts every message with id > the pre-register tail is delivered exactly once and in ascending order. The existing GC-recovery tests only exercise injection well after subscribe() resolved, so none of them can fire on this window.

summary: `waiters.set(topic, …)` is published before the awaited tail probe (and before `void loop()`), so any failure or disconnect after that point leaves a waiter set with no loop behind it; a later blocking fetchRecent piggybacks on the dead set and parks for the full blockMs instead of waking on the message.
failure: Reproduced: post 'old', take the tail cursor, `fake.failNextMessagesRead()`, `await plugin.subscribe(topic, …)` rejects (502 on the tail probe), then `fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 3000})` with a post 100ms later returned after 3011ms instead of ~100ms. The same shape occurs if `disconnect()` races the awaited `register()`/tail probe: `waiters.clear()` runs first, then line 339 re-publishes a set that survives the disconnect. The comment on lines 337-338 explicitly claims this class is already guarded ("Seeded AFTER a successful register so a register failure leaves no dead waiter set") — it guards only the register throw, not the two later ones.
remediation: Publish the waiter set only at the point the loop is actually running (immediately before `void loop()`, after every await), and remove it in a `finally`/on loop exit and on any subscribe failure; also re-check `this.stopped` before publishing so a raced disconnect cannot resurrect it.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a topic is only advertised as piggyback-able while a live loop is draining it'. Parameterize a test over every await inside subscribe() (register, tail probe) × {throws, disconnect fires}, asserting afterwards that a blocking fetchRecent with blockMs=3000 either wakes within ~500ms of a concurrent post or does not consult the piggyback path at all. Note that no existing test covers the piggyback path at all — the conformance blockMs case never calls subscribe, so it exercises only the dedicated-queue branch.

summary: `fetchMessages` passes the caller's `limit` straight into `num_before`/`num_after`, but real Zulip rejects `num_before + num_after > 5000` with HTTP 400, so any large-page fetch throws instead of returning a page.
failure: `fetchRecent({ topic, limit: 10_000 })` → `GET /api/v1/messages?...num_before=10000` → real Zulip raises `JsonableError("Too many messages requested (maximum 5000).")` (traced in upstream zerver/views/message_fetch.py: `MAX_MESSAGES_PER_FETCH = 5000`; `if num_of_messages_requested > MAX_MESSAGES_PER_FETCH: raise`), which `fetchWithRetry` turns into a thrown Error. That is exactly what the shared suite does — `packages/conformance/src/index.ts:11` `drainAll(..., 10_000)` and line 151 `limit: 10_000` — so the env-gated real-server run advertised in this package's README (and in the root README's `fake-conformance + operator-run` claim) cannot pass. Core also permits `catchup.limit` of any positive int (bridge-core/src/config.ts:122), so a configured 6000 breaks every catch-up.
remediation: Clamp `limit` to Zulip's 5000 per request inside `fetchMessages` and paginate transparently (loop on the last returned id) so the seam's `limit` stays honest, rather than propagating a server error the caller cannot interpret.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'plugin must not forward a caller page size that exceeds the backend's documented maximum'. Teach the fake to enforce the real 5000 cap (400 when num_before+num_after>5000) and add a parameterized case over limits {1, 100, 5000, 5001, 10_000, 50_000} asserting fetchRecent returns min(limit, available) messages ascending and never throws — the same table can be reused for every HTTP backend with a documented page cap.

summary: Zulip matches topics case-INsensitively on both the read narrow and the event-queue narrow, while Parley's allowlist and topic identity are exact strings — so a message posted to a case variant of an allowlisted topic is delivered as if it were the allowlisted topic, and two distinct Parley topics differing only in case share one history.
failure: Config allowlists topic `ops`. A third party (or another session) posts to the Zulip topic `OPS` in the same stream. Traced in upstream Zulip: `zerver/lib/topic.py:410 topic_match_q → Q(subject__iexact=topic_name)` for `GET /api/v1/messages`, and `zerver/lib/narrow_predicate.py` for the event queue (`if operand.lower() != topic_name.lower()`). Result: `fetchRecent({topic: asTopic('ops')})` returns the `OPS` message and `subscribe('ops')` pushes it, with `zulipToMessage` stamping `topic: 'ops'` — the allowlist is bypassed by case and topic isolation is silently violated. Conversely `topics: ['Alpha','alpha']` are one namespace on the wire.
remediation: Canonicalize the topic on the wire (e.g. lower-case it in `post`, the narrow, and `register`) so Parley's namespace maps 1:1 onto Zulip's case-folded one, and reject/collapse configs whose topics collide case-insensitively at connect; document the folding in the README's 'one inexactness' section alongside the mutable-topic caveat.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'backend namespace folding must not widen the topic allowlist'. Make the fake fold topic (and stream) comparisons the way the server does, then add a parameterized isolation case over variant pairs {('ops','OPS'), ('a b','a  b') where applicable, ('t','T')} asserting either that the two names are rejected as colliding or that a message posted to one never surfaces under the other. The existing 'topics are isolated' conformance case uses random distinct names and can never fire on a folding collision.

summary: Zulip truncates topic names to 60 characters on send, but the plugin narrows reads and event queues on the untruncated name, so posting to a topic longer than 60 chars succeeds and is then invisible to fetchRecent and subscribe.
failure: `post(asTopic('a'.repeat(70)), …)` returns a real message id (Zulip stamps the message with a 60-char truncated subject — traced upstream: `zerver/actions/message_send.py:1774 topic_name = truncate_topic(topic_name)` → `truncate_content(topic_name, MAX_TOPIC_NAME_LENGTH=60, TOPIC_TRUNCATION_MESSAGE)`), while `fetchRecent({topic: 'a'.repeat(70)})` narrows on the 70-char operand and returns `[]` forever, and `subscribe` on that topic never fires. Two long topics sharing a 57-char prefix additionally merge into one. No error signals any of it — a silent write-only hole, the repo's named fail-fast defect class.
remediation: Fail fast: validate at `connect`/`post`/`subscribe` that the effective Zulip topic is <= 60 characters (throwing a clear error naming the limit), or deterministically map long Parley topics to a stable <=60-char Zulip topic (e.g. prefix + hash) used consistently by post, narrow and register.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'the backend must not silently rewrite the addressing key'. Have the fake apply the real 60-char truncation on POST, and add a parameterized round-trip case over topic lengths {1, 59, 60, 61, 200} and over two long topics with a shared 57-char prefix, asserting each post is either rejected with a clear error or read back under the exact topic it was posted to, with no cross-topic bleed.

summary: The in-process fake is strict only about form-encoding; it accepts any page size, matches topics exactly and case-sensitively, never truncates topics, and accepts any credentials — so the whole green suite is compatible with four distinct real-server failures.
failure: Against the fake, `fetchRecent({limit: 10_000})`, `post` to a 70-char topic, a topic differing only in case, and a wrong `api_key` all behave perfectly; against a real Zulip they yield a 400 'Too many messages requested', a write-only topic, cross-topic delivery, and a 401 respectively (see the four findings above). The README's claim that setting `PARLEY_ZULIP_*` 'additionally run[s] the same suite against a real server' is therefore untested and, as of today, would fail on the first `drainAll`.
remediation: Encode the documented server constraints in the fake — reject num_before+num_after>5000, fold topic/stream comparison to lower-case, truncate subjects to 60 chars on POST, and validate the Basic credentials against a configured pair — so the fake is a semantic model of the API rather than a permissive echo.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'every real-server constraint the plugin must respect is expressed in the fake'. Add a `serverConstraints` table (max page, topic max length, topic case folding, auth) that both the fake reads and a set of parameterized plugin tests assert against, so adding a constraint automatically produces a failing test until the plugin honours it — and mirror the same table into the other HTTP-backend fakes.

summary: Every non-recoverable subscribe failure (auth revoked, stream unsubscribed, any non-BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID error, repeated register failure) is retried forever at a flat 200ms with no backoff escalation and no diagnostic, so a permanently dead push path looks identical to a healthy idle one while hammering the server at ~5 req/s.
failure: Revoke the bot's API key while subscribed: `GET /api/v1/events` returns 401, `http()` throws, the catch at line 385-388 does `delay(200); continue` and loops indefinitely; the operator sees no stderr line and `parley_list_users`/live push simply stop working. Same loop for a permanently failing `register()` (line 406-409) and for any other 400 code (line 410-412). Contrast `packages/bridge-slack/src/index.ts:418-426`, which uses capped exponential backoff for the same situation.
remediation: Use capped exponential backoff (200ms → 5s) for the loop's error paths and emit a rate-limited `console.error` naming the failure after N consecutive failures, so a dead push path is visible and cheap rather than invisible and hot.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a persistently failing background loop must back off and must be observable'. Add a parameterized test over failure modes {401 on /events, 500 on /events, register always throws, non-queue 400} that runs the loop against a counting fake for ~2s and asserts (a) the request count grows sub-linearly (backoff engaged, e.g. < 15 attempts) and (b) at least one stderr diagnostic naming the backend was emitted.

summary: `resolveIdentity` matches a handle against `full_name` — a user-settable, non-unique display name — with `find`, so the first member in server order wins and any realm user can make themselves the resolution target for another participant's handle.
failure: Realm has `{user_id: 42, full_name: 'Pat Sharp'}` (an ordinary member who set that name) ordered before the genuine `{user_id: 11, full_name: 'Pat Sharp'}`; `resolveIdentity(asHandle('Pat Sharp'))` returns `backendRef: '42'`. Zulip permits duplicate full names unless the realm opts into `require_unique_names`, and deactivated users are also in `/api/v1/users`. (Impact is currently bounded: nothing in bridge-core consumes `backendRef` — an email-shaped full_name is impossible because '@' is in Zulip's NAME_INVALID_CHARS — so this is a latent, not live, spoof.)
remediation: Resolve on `email` (and optionally `user_id`) only, treating `full_name` as a last-resort match that is rejected when it is ambiguous (more than one active member matches) rather than silently taking the first; skip `is_active: false` members.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'identity resolution never silently picks among ambiguous candidates'. Parameterize the fake's member directory over {unique email match, two members sharing a full_name, a deactivated member matching, a member whose full_name equals another member's handle} and assert the plugin resolves the exact-email match, and for the ambiguous cases either throws or degrades to the string convention — never picks arbitrarily by list order.

summary: `disconnect()` awaits a best-effort `DELETE /api/v1/events` per live queue with no AbortSignal and no timeout, so an unreachable-but-not-refusing server can stall shutdown for undici's default 300s header timeout per queue.
failure: Zulip host becomes a black hole (packets dropped, connection stays open) while two queues are live; `bridge.shutdown()` from the CLI's SIGTERM/stdin-EOF handler (`packages/bridge-zulip/src/cli.ts:43`) never returns within the container's grace period, so the process is SIGKILLed instead of exiting cleanly — the same orphan-cleanup problem BUG-38 was added to solve.
remediation: Give the teardown deletes an `AbortSignal.timeout(~2s)` (they are already `.catch`-swallowed and Zulip GCs queues after ~10 min anyway) and issue them concurrently with `Promise.allSettled` rather than sequentially.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'teardown completes in bounded time regardless of backend responsiveness'. Add a parameterized disconnect test over server states {responsive, 500s, hangs forever, connection reset, closed socket} × {0, 1, 5 live queues} asserting `disconnect()` resolves within a fixed budget (e.g. 3s) in every combination.

summary: The plugin warns loudly about the default API key but says nothing when a real bot key is sent as HTTP Basic over a plaintext `http://` URL to a non-loopback host, and the README never states that `site_url` should be https.
