failure: `backend_config: { site_url: 'http://zulip.example.com', email: 'bot@…', api_key: 's3cret-real-key' }` connects happily and puts `Authorization: Basic <base64 email:key>` on every request in cleartext across the network, with no warning — while the strictly less dangerous default-key case does warn. The README's reverse-proxy section discusses forwarding headers but never TLS for the bot credential.
remediation: Warn (or refuse, matching the repo's fail-fast posture) at `connect` when `site_url` is `http://` and the host is not loopback, and add a one-line TLS note to the README config table next to `site_url`.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'credentials are never transmitted in the clear without an explicit operator signal'. Parameterize the existing SEC-06 warning suite over `site_url` × `api_key` — {http loopback, http remote host, https remote} × {default key, real key} — asserting exactly which combinations must warn; the current creds-warning test only varies the key and would stay green if the transport check were deleted.

summary: The gateway open has no handshake timeout: if the socket connects and HELLO arrives but READY never does, `openSocket`'s promise never settles. `subscribe()` hangs forever (bridge startup never completes, no error), and every blocking `fetchRecent` hangs unboundedly because it `await this.ensureGateway()` before arming its blockMs timer — so `block_ms` is silently ignored and the core-mandated `catchup.block_max_ms` cap that exists to keep a blocked call under the client tool timeout is bypassed.
failure: Reproduced with a mocked `ws`: connect({gateway_url}), then the fake server sends op 10 HELLO, plugin sends op 2 IDENTIFY, server sends nothing further. `plugin.subscribe(asTopic('1'), fn)` is still pending after 1s of real time (and forever). Separately `plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since, blockMs: 100})` is still pending after 1500ms — 15x its own budget. Same shape in production when Discord accepts the TCP/WS connection but the IDENTIFY is dropped, or a proxy blackholes the response.
remediation: Race the `openSocket` promise against a bounded handshake deadline (a few seconds, config-overridable): on expiry `ws.terminate()`, reject, and let `ensureGateway`'s catch clear `gatewayReady` so the caller degrades. In `fetchRecent`, additionally bound the `ensureGateway()` await by the remaining `blockMs` (Promise.race with the block timer) so the long-poll budget is a hard ceiling on the whole call, not just on the post-connect wait. Also give the first open the same bounded retry the post-READY path has, instead of rejecting `subscribe()` and killing the process on one blip.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven 'gateway never completes the handshake' suite over the stall points — {no TCP open, open-but-no-HELLO, HELLO-but-no-READY, READY-then-silence} x {subscribe, fetchRecent(blockMs), resolveIdentity} — asserting every entry point settles within a bounded multiple of its declared budget under fake timers. The existing gateway-reconnect.test.ts only ever drives sockets that promptly HELLO and READY (reachReady() always calls ws.hello()), so no current test can observe a stalled handshake; a 'FakeWs that ignores IDENTIFY' variant belongs in the same table.

summary: A terminal gateway close (4004/4010–4014) that happens AFTER the socket reached READY is swallowed entirely: `ready` is true so the `reject(...)` branch is skipped, `scheduleReconnect` is deliberately not called, and the plugin has no logger. The bridge keeps running, keeps answering MCP tools, keeps heart-beating itself into every peer's roster as reachable — and never delivers another live message.
failure: Bridge starts, gateway READY, live push works. An admin then toggles off the MESSAGE CONTENT privileged intent (or rotates/invalidates the bot token). Discord closes with 4014 (or 4004). Close handler: clears the heartbeat, sets `this.gatewayReady = undefined`, `if (!ready)` is false → returns. Nothing is thrown, nothing is logged, `subs` still holds every topic, `startPushLoop` already ran and never calls `subscribe` again. Result: live push is permanently dead and silently so; the operator's only signal is 'messages stopped arriving'.
remediation: Surface terminal closes on the post-READY path: take an injected `onFatal`/logger in `connect()` (or write to stderr as the CLI does) and emit the close code and its meaning; optionally mark the plugin unhealthy so a subsequent blocking `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` fails fast with that reason instead of silently opening a fresh socket that will be closed again. Fail-fast/no-silent-no-op applies here even though not retrying is the correct rate-limit posture.
testUpgrade: Parameterize over TERMINAL_CLOSE = [4004,4010,4011,4012,4013,4014] x {before READY, after READY} and assert that in BOTH phases the failure is observable — pre-READY via a rejection, post-READY via the injected fatal callback — and that no attempt-storm follows. The current BUG-07 test only covers the post-READY 4014 case and asserts only the absence of re-IDENTIFYs, so 'silently does nothing' passes it; the class to lock is 'a terminal backend failure is never invisible', not 'the loop stops'.

summary: The reconnect backoff caps at 60s and the plugin deliberately never RESUMEs, so a chronically flapping (but non-terminal) gateway re-IDENTIFYs roughly every 60–61s indefinitely: ~1416 IDENTIFYs per 24h against Discord's documented 1000-per-24h limit, whose penalty is a bot-token RESET. That is precisely the harm the BUG-07 comment block at lines 61–68 and 507–513 claims this code prevents.
failure: Sustained non-terminal flap (close 1006/4000/4008/4009 shortly after READY, e.g. a degraded network path or a gateway shard cycling). `Math.min(1000 * 2 ** n, 60_000) + jitter<=1000` saturates at <=61s within ~6 attempts and never grows further; 86400/61 ≈ 1416 IDENTIFYs in 24h > 1000 → Discord resets the token → every Parley instance sharing that bot stops working until a human re-provisions.
remediation: Raise the cap above 86.4s (e.g. 120s) so the steady-state rate is structurally under 1000/day, and/or count IDENTIFYs in a rolling 24h window and hard-stop (with the same surfaced-fatal treatment as finding 2) before the quota. Better still, implement RESUME (op 6 with session_id + `resume_gateway_url` from READY): resumes do not consume the IDENTIFY budget, and the 'no RESUME because catch-up reconciles' rationale addresses correctness, not quota.
testUpgrade: A property test over the backoff generator rather than the observed first delays: for a simulated 24h of continuous flapping, assert the number of op-2 frames sent stays under the provider quota (parameterize quota/window so the same case guards any provider-rate-limited handshake — Slack Socket Mode and Telegram getUpdates have sibling budgets). The existing 'backoff grows and is capped at 60s' test asserts the cap that causes the problem, so it would stay green through the fix.

summary: The seam gives a plugin exactly two legal answers for a topic with no backend representation: an empty page with a replayable cursor, or `NoSuchTopicError`. Discord's `fetchRecent` gives neither — an unknown/inaccessible channel yields a raw `Error('Discord GET /channels/... → 404: {...}')` from `fetchWithRetry`. Core explicitly branches on `NoSuchTopicError` (transport/tools.ts:327) to return an empty roster, so `parley_list_users` fails with an HTTP stack trace instead of an empty roster whenever the presence channel does not exist.
failure: Reproduced: plugin connected with an api_url whose channel route 404s, `fetchRecent({topic: asTopic('123')})` rejects with `Error: Discord GET /channels/123/messages?limit=100 → 404: {"message":"Not Found","code":0}`, name 'Error'. In production this is the default configuration: presence.topic defaults to 'parley-presence', which as a Discord channel id is Unknown Channel (10003) → every `parley_list_users` call throws. Same for any configured topic whose channel was deleted or the bot lost access to.
remediation: Have `http()` pass `allowStatuses: [404]` (or catch and inspect) on the channel-messages GET and translate Discord error code 10003 (Unknown Channel) — and arguably 50001 Missing Access — into `new NoSuchTopicError(topic)`. Leave every other non-2xx propagating as a real failure.
testUpgrade: Extend the shared conformance suite with an 'absent topic' case each backend must satisfy: `fetchRecent` on a topic the backend genuinely cannot represent must either return `{messages: [], nextCursor}` that replays, or reject with `instanceof NoSuchTopicError` — never any other error type. Drive it from a context hook that lets each backend produce a genuinely-absent topic (for Discord, a channel id the fake rejects with 404/10003), so the case is parameterized over backends rather than being a Discord-only regression test.

summary: The in-process fake makes every channel id valid and every request succeed: `channels.get(channelId) ?? []` returns 200 with an empty array for any id, it never emits 404/403/429/400, never enforces Discord's 100-per-page or 2000-char limits as errors, and never closes a socket with a gateway code. So the whole error/edge half of the plugin — the 404→absent-topic contract, the 429 retry path the README advertises, oversized-content rejection, and any REST failure during a blocking fetch — is untested and any mutation there stays green.
failure: The conformance case 'fetchRecent on a never-posted topic returns an empty page with a replayable cursor' passes for Discord only because the fake invents a 200 `[]` for a channel that does not exist; against real Discord that same input throws (finding 4). Deleting the entire `readRetryAfter` implementation and replacing it with `return 500` also keeps the suite green, because no fake response is ever a 429.
remediation: Give the fake a channel registry: ids must be created (or listed in an allowlist) before they resolve, unknown ids return `404 {"message":"Unknown Channel","code":10003}`, and add scriptable fault injection — a per-request queue of {status, headers, body} the test can prime with 429 (header and body `retry_after` variants), 403 Missing Access, and 400 content-too-long. Expose a hook to force gateway close codes so the REST fake and the reconnect suite exercise the same plugin rather than two disjoint mocks.
testUpgrade: Table-driven 'server says no' cases over {404 unknown channel, 403 missing access, 429 header-only, 429 body-only, 429 with retry_after far beyond the 5s cap, 400 content too long, 500} x {post, fetchRecent, fetchRecent(blockMs), resolveIdentity}, asserting the exact classified outcome (NoSuchTopicError / typed throw / bounded retry count) per cell. Guarding the class 'the fake can express every failure the real API can' also prevents the next backend's fake from being written as a happy-path echo.

summary: `subs` is keyed by Discord channel id, and `channelId()` is an unchecked many-to-one map (two `channel_map` entries may name the same channel, or a mapped id may equal another topic's literal string). The second `subscribe` silently overwrites the first: the earlier topic's handler is dropped with no error, and messages posted to that topic are delivered to the live path labeled with the OTHER topic. Core has `topic-name.ts::safeName` precisely to make topic→backend-name folds injective (BUG-14/SEC-07); Discord's fold has no equivalent guard.
failure: Reproduced: channel_map {alpha: '777', beta: '777'}; subscribe('alpha'), subscribe('beta'), then post to topic 'alpha'. Observed `alpha got []  beta got ['hello']` — topic alpha's subscription is silently gone and alpha's traffic is mislabeled as beta, which also mis-routes core's per-topic seen-set and mention filter.
remediation: Detect the collision at `connect()` and fail fast: reject a `channel_map` whose values are not distinct, and reject a mapping whose target collides with another configured topic's literal form. If aliasing is genuinely wanted, make `subs` a `Map<string, Set<{topic, handler}>>` and fan out per subscribed topic — but per DESIGN's strictness-at-the-seam rule, rejecting is the better default.
testUpgrade: Add a shared 'topic aliasing' conformance-adjacent case for every backend with a name/id mapping (discord, slack, telegram, zulip, matrix, nats, xmpp): given two distinct topics whose mapping collides, subscribing to both must either reject at config load or deliver each message exactly once to EACH subscriber under ITS OWN topic — never silently drop one. Parameterize over collision shapes {explicit duplicate map values, mapped-vs-literal collision, case/charset-fold collision} so the sibling of safeName's lossy-fold case is covered too.

summary: The no-`since` default-window path clamps to `Math.min(limit, 100)` and returns `nextCursor` = the NEWEST id. A caller asking for more than 100 silently gets the newest 100 and a cursor past everything older — those older messages are then permanently unreachable via the cursor path, with no signal that truncation happened. Discord's `before=` parameter would let the plugin page backwards to honour the requested limit, as the `since` path already pages forward.
failure: Reproduced: post 150 messages to one channel, then `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 1000})` → 100 messages beginning at 'm50'; 'm0'..'m49' are dropped and `nextCursor` is the id of 'm149', so no subsequent `since` query can ever reach them. A fresh instance with `catchup.limit: 200` therefore starts mid-history and reports nothing wrong.
remediation: Page backwards with `before=<oldest id so far>` until `limit` is satisfied or the channel head is reached, mirroring the forward paging in `fetchSince`; or, if the 100-message window is intentional, make it explicit rather than silent (clamp `limit` visibly and document that the no-`since` window is capped at 100 in both the README table and the JSDoc).
testUpgrade: Parameterize the conformance 'default window' and 'multi-process writes' cases over message counts that straddle every backend's native page cap — e.g. counts [1, cap-1, cap, cap+1, 3*cap+7] and limits [1, cap, 10*cap] — asserting that `fetchRecent({limit: N})` on a topic with M messages returns min(N, M) messages ending at the newest. Today the concurrency case is 4x25 = exactly 100, which happens to equal Discord's page cap, so it is green by coincidence and a widened generator (5x25) would fail it.

summary: Discord caps a bot message at 2000 characters, and the plugin neither chunks nor pre-validates: `post` of a longer body gets a raw `Error: Discord POST /channels/<id>/messages → 400: {"message":"Invalid Form Body"...}`. Parley's headline use case is context sharing and task hand-off, where >2000-character posts are routine, yet neither the README's `post` row, the config table, nor the class JSDoc mentions the limit — so a user reasonably predicts the same behaviour they get from SQLite/Redis/Matrix.
failure: `parley_post({topic, content})` with a 2500-character handoff summary → HTTP 400 from Discord → the MCP tool call fails with an opaque Invalid Form Body error; the agent has no way to know a length limit exists or what it is. (Traced through `post` → `http` → `fetchWithRetry`, which throws on any non-2xx; not reproduced against the live API because the fake never enforces the limit — hence PLAUSIBLE.)
remediation: Validate length in `post` and throw an actionable, plugin-authored error naming the 2000-character Discord limit and the actual length, rather than relaying Discord's form-body blob; and document the limit prominently in the README's positioning/seam-mapping section next to the other hosted-SaaS caveats. Do not silently chunk — that would break the one-post/one-backendMsgId contract.
testUpgrade: A cross-backend table of provider payload limits ({discord: 2000, telegram: 4096, slack: 40000, matrix/xmpp/sqlite: none}) driving a parameterized case: posting at limit-1, exactly limit, and limit+1 must either succeed or reject with an error whose message contains the numeric limit — never an unclassified upstream 4xx body. This also requires the fake to enforce the limit (see the fake-fidelity finding).

summary: Presence is ON by default in core (`presence.enabled: true`, `presence.topic: 'parley-presence'`), and on Discord a topic string IS a channel id — so the out-of-the-box configuration posts every hello/heartbeat/goodbye to a channel named 'parley-presence' that cannot exist. Those posts fail and are swallowed by the presence loop, and `parley_list_users` throws a raw 404 (finding 4). The README documents `token`, `api_url`, `gateway_url` and `channel_map` but says nothing about presence needing a real channel id or a `channel_map` entry.
failure: Run `parley-discord --config parley.config.yaml` with a config that only sets `identity`, `topics` and `backend_config.token`. Every 10 minutes the bridge silently 404s a heartbeat (presence-loop.ts swallows the rejection), the peer never appears in anyone's roster, and calling `parley_list_users` from this instance rejects with `Discord GET /channels/parley-presence/messages?limit=... → 404`. Nothing in the logs explains why.
remediation: Document in the README (and ideally validate at `connect()`): with Discord either set `presence.enabled: false`, or map `presence.topic` through `channel_map` to a real channel id, or set `presence.topic` to a channel id directly. A `connect()`-time shape check on configured topic→channel ids (Discord ids are 17–20 digit snowflakes) that warns on stderr for non-snowflake, unmapped topics would turn a silent 10-minute-repeating failure into a startup diagnostic.
testUpgrade: A per-backend 'default config smoke' case in the shared suite: build the bridge with a minimal config that omits every optional knob and assert that (a) no seam call rejects and (b) `parley_list_users` returns a roster envelope rather than throwing. Parameterized over backends, this guards the class 'a backend whose topics are opaque provider ids silently breaks core features that assume human-named topics' — which also applies to Slack and Telegram.

summary: `readRetryAfter` caps Discord's `retry_after` at 5000ms and `fetchWithRetry` loops without any attempt ceiling, so a 429 asking for 60s (global rate limit) or an hour (Cloudflare ban response) is retried every 5s forever — the plugin hammers exactly the endpoint that told it to stop, escalating a temporary rate limit toward an IP-level ban. The README's claim that 'the plugin honors 429 retry_after automatically' is true only for waits under 5s.
failure: Discord replies `429 {"global": true, "retry_after": 60.0}` (or Cloudflare's 1015 with `Retry-After: 3600`). `Math.min(Math.ceil(60*1000), 5000)` = 5000, so the plugin re-issues the same request 12 times inside the window Discord asked it to stay silent — and keeps going indefinitely, since the only exit is `isStopped()` (disconnect) or a non-429 response.
remediation: Honour the server's value up to a much larger ceiling (e.g. the caller's remaining budget, or 60–120s) rather than 5s, and add an attempt/total-elapsed ceiling after which the call rejects with a classified rate-limit error. The 5s cap is the shared `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` contract, so raising it is a cross-plugin change — which makes it a seam-level fix to surface, not a Discord-local branch; note that the same inversion exists in every HTTP backend using that helper.
testUpgrade: A parameterized 429 table over retry_after values [0.1, 1, 5, 30, 3600] x {header only, body only, both, malformed} asserting the observed wait equals min(server value, documented ceiling) and that the total number of requests inside the server-requested window is 1. Run it against every net-util consumer from a shared helper so the ceiling policy is verified once per backend rather than reasoned about per plugin.

summary: The `since` path trims `collected` to the oldest `limit + 200` RAW entries before filtering out non-plain subtypes. If that raw tail happens to contain no plain messages, fetchRecent returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` — the caller's cursor never advances, so catch-up livelocks and the real messages behind the system records are never delivered, ever.
failure: Channel seeded with 400 `channel_join` records followed by 50 real messages; `fetchRecent({since: asCursor('0'), limit: 100})` → `{messages: [], nextCursor: '0'}`. Feeding that nextCursor back yields the identical empty page forever. The 50 real messages are permanently unreachable. (Reproduced against test/fake-slack.ts.) This is the same class BUG-31 fixed on the no-`since` branch and left unfixed on the `since` branch.
remediation: Make the retained tail plain-message-aware: trim on the count of `isPlainMessage` entries rather than raw entries (keep raw pages but retain the oldest N raw whose plain count >= limit), or drop the trim and filter each page before accumulating. Additionally, when the returned window is empty but the walk saw entries strictly after `since`, advance `nextCursor` to the oldest observed raw `ts` so progress is guaranteed and no plain message can sit below it.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a single table-driven case over the CLASS 'catch-up must make progress whatever the subtype mix': generate channel layouts as a list of (count, subtype|plain) runs — leading-system-heavy, trailing-system-heavy, alternating, all-system, all-plain, run lengths straddling limit, limit+200 and 2*limit — cross-producted with `since` in {undefined, '0', mid-channel tail} and limit in {1, 10, 100}. Assert for every layout: repeated fetchRecent looping on nextCursor terminates and yields exactly the full ordered set of plain messages after `since`, and nextCursor is non-decreasing. The existing BUG-31 test is too narrow (no-`since` only) and BUG-18's test seeds only plain messages, so neither can see this.

summary: `ensureSocket()` does `this.wsReady ??= this.openSocket()`. When `openSocket` rejects inside the `apps.connections.open` Web API call (before any WebSocket exists), nothing clears `wsReady`, so the REJECTED promise is memoized. Every later `subscribe()` and every blocking `fetchRecent` replays the cached rejection without touching the network — one transient failure disables the live path for the whole process lifetime.
failure: HTTP fake returns `{ok:false, error:'internal_error'}` for the first `apps.connections.open` and `{ok:true,...}` thereafter. Three sequential `subscribe()` calls all throw `Slack apps.connections.open → internal_error`, and the server records exactly ONE apps.connections.open hit — attempts 2 and 3 never reached the wire. Result: live push never recovers, and `fetchRecent({blockMs})` silently degrades to the non-blocking path forever (its ensureSocket is inside a swallowing try/catch).
remediation: Never memoize a rejection: `const p = this.openSocket(); this.wsReady = p; p.catch(() => { if (this.wsReady === p) this.wsReady = undefined; });` — mirroring the pattern already used for `authTestPromise` (line 321), which explicitly de-memoizes failure. Consider also routing a failed initial connect into the same backoff `reconnect()` loop the post-hello close path uses.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a lazily-memoized async singleton must not cache failure' with a parameterized case over every memoized promise in the plugin (`wsReady`, `authTestPromise`) x failure mode (`ok:false` body, HTTP 500, socket error, pre-hello close): drive the operation N times against a fake that fails the first K attempts and succeeds after, and assert (a) the underlying endpoint was hit N times, not once, and (b) attempt K+1 succeeds. The BUG-30 test only exercises the pre-hello-CLOSE path, which does clear wsReady, so it cannot see the API-failure path.

summary: `openSocket()` awaits `apps.connections.open`, then constructs the WebSocket and assigns `this.ws = ws` with no re-check of `this.stopped`. A `disconnect()` that lands during that await clears `this.ws`/`this.wsReady` first, and the in-flight open then installs a live socket onto a disconnected plugin. The 'close' handler refuses to act (`this.stopped` is true), so the socket is never closed.
failure: `plugin.subscribe(t, ...)` immediately followed by `await plugin.disconnect()`; 300 ms later the plugin's internal `ws.readyState` is 1 (OPEN). The socket outlives disconnect, holds an open handle (can keep the process from exiting), and consumes one of the ~10 concurrent Socket Mode connections per app token that this package's own README calls out as scarce. Repeated connect/disconnect cycles exhaust the app-token budget.
remediation: After every await in `openSocket`, re-check `this.stopped` (and that `this.wsReady` still belongs to this attempt) before assigning `this.ws`; if stopped, close the freshly opened socket and reject/return. Same guard applies inside the `new Promise` before wiring handlers.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'teardown racing an in-flight async resource acquisition must leave nothing open' with a fuzz/parameterized test: for delay d in {0, 1, 5, 20, 50, 120} ms, start `subscribe()` (and, separately, a blocking `fetchRecent`) then call `disconnect()` after d ms; assert the fake server observes zero live Socket Mode connections and zero open HTTP sockets after settling, for every d. The current suite never calls disconnect() concurrently with an in-flight subscribe.

summary: `api()` turns every `ok:false` into a generic `Error`, so Slack's `channel_not_found` never becomes the seam's `NoSuchTopicError`. The seam JSDoc (bridge-core/src/seam.ts:119) names exactly this case ('a chat channel that does not exist') and core (transport/tools.ts:327) branches on it. Because the default presence topic `parley-presence` is not a channel id and `channelFor` passes unmapped topics through as channel-id literals, an out-of-the-box Slack deployment hits this on the presence topic on every call.
failure: With a server returning `{ok:false, error:'channel_not_found'}`, `fetchRecent({topic: asTopic('parley-presence')})` throws `Error: Slack conversations.history → channel_not_found` (not NoSuchTopicError). Downstream: `parley_list_users` rethrows instead of returning the empty roster core intends, so the tool is hard-broken on a default Slack config; and every presence beat's `post` fails into presence-loop's silent `.catch(() => {})`, so the bridge is invisible to every peer with no diagnostic anywhere.
remediation: Map Slack's absent-conversation errors (`channel_not_found`, and `not_in_channel` for fetch) to `NoSuchTopicError(topic)` in `fetchRecent` (and consider it for `post`). Separately, document in the README that `presence.topic` must be mapped in `channel_map` to a real channel id (or presence disabled), since `parley-presence` is never a valid Slack channel id.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'backend absent-topic errors map to the seam's absent-topic contract' by extending FakeSlack to model unknown channels the way slack.com does (`ok:false, error:'channel_not_found'` instead of today's `ok:true, messages:[]`), then add a parameterized case over {fetchRecent, post} x {channel_not_found, not_in_channel, is_archived} asserting `NoSuchTopicError` for the absent cases and a plain Error for genuine failures (`invalid_auth`, `ratelimited`). The conformance suite's 'never-posted topic returns an empty page' case currently passes only because the fake fabricates an empty success for unknown channels — a false green.

summary: Two load-bearing invariants have no test that can fail. (1) `compareTs` — the function DESIGN §6 singles out for Slack ('compared integer-wise, never as float/lexical') — is exported but has no unit test; replacing its whole body with `Number(a) - Number(b)` (the exact defect the docs warn about) keeps all 16 tests green. (2) The live-path subtype guard in `onEnvelope` never fires: FakeSlack's push path only emits plain messages, so deleting `!isPlainMessage(event)` from the envelope router also keeps all 16 tests green.
failure: Mutation 1: `compareTs` → naive float compare ⇒ `npx vitest run packages/bridge-slack` = 16 passed. Mutation 2: drop the `isPlainMessage` check in `onEnvelope` ⇒ 16 passed. So a regression that pushes `message_changed`/`message_deleted` mutation records into the `<channel>` path — breaking dedup with a duplicate `ts` carrying different content — ships undetected, as does a cursor comparator that loses precision on real 16-digit Slack `ts` values.
remediation: Add a direct unit test for `compareTs` over adversarial vectors (identical seconds with differing suffixes, 16-significant-digit values whose float parse collides, '0' sentinel, suffix-less input, large second values). Teach FakeSlack to push subtyped and mutation envelopes (`message_changed`, `message_deleted`, `channel_join`, `bot_message`) over the socket and assert only plain/bot_message reach the handler.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'every documented invariant must have a mutation-detectable test' with (a) a table-driven `compareTs` case whose vectors include pairs that a float comparator orders wrongly — e.g. ('1700000000.000001','1700000000.000002') parsed as doubles — plus a property check that sorting a shuffled minted-ts sequence recovers insertion order; and (b) a parameterized live-path filter case over every subtype the fake can emit, asserting the surfaced set equals {undefined, 'bot_message'} on BOTH the push path and the history path (today only the history path is covered, by BUG-31).

summary: Because the `since` path walks to cursor exhaustion on every call but returns only `limit` messages, draining a backlog costs ~backlog²/(2·limit·page) requests, not the O(backlog/page) the JSDoc advertises 'for one call'. The doc describes the per-call cost and never states that the next call re-walks the same shrinking backlog.
failure: Measured against FakeSlack (page=50): draining a 2000-message backlog with limit=100 took 421 `conversations.history` requests versus a 40-request floor. Scaled to real Slack (page=200), a 20k-message backlog costs ~10,000 requests; at Slack's tiered rate limits that is hours of 429-throttled paging to catch up one topic, and it repeats on every bridge restart that resumes from an old cursor.
remediation: Bound the walk with `latest` (fetch the window above `since` in oldest-first fashion by narrowing `latest` downward), or cache the resolved pagination position per (channel, since) across the immediately-following calls, or raise the effective page/limit when a large backlog is detected. At minimum, correct the JSDoc and README to state the aggregate drain cost and recommend a large `catchup.limit` on Slack.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'catch-up drain cost must stay near-linear in backlog' with a parameterized cost assertion: for backlog in {200, 1000, 4000} and limit in {50, 100}, count backend requests while looping fetchRecent to exhaustion and assert requests <= C · backlog/page (a linear bound), so any quadratic re-walk — in this backend or a future paging change — trips the test rather than only slowing CI.

summary: `compareTs`'s JSDoc justifies integer-wise suffix comparison with 'NOT lexically ordered (suffix widths could differ)'. If suffix widths genuinely could differ, comparing suffixes as integers is also wrong — and wrong in a way lexical comparison would get right. The stated reason does not support the implementation.
failure: `compareTs('1.1', '1.000002')` returns -1, i.e. it claims `1.1` sorts BEFORE `1.000002`, which is false as a time comparison (0.1 s > 0.000002 s). Today this is latent only because real Slack always emits 6-digit suffixes — the code is correct for the actual data and the comment's premise is what is false, which is exactly the kind of comment that licenses a wrong 'fix' later.
remediation: Either state the real invariant ('Slack ts suffixes are fixed-width 6 digits; integer comparison of the suffix is exact and avoids the float precision loss of Number(ts)') and, for fail-fast, assert/normalize the suffix width; or make the comparator width-correct by zero-padding both suffixes to a common length before the integer compare.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'comparator comments must match comparator behaviour' with a table-driven comparator test that includes unequal-width suffixes as explicit expectations — whichever semantics the team chooses, the vectors pin it, so a future reader cannot flip the implementation on the strength of a stale comment.

summary: `post()` discards `identity` (src/index.ts:169) and Slack stamps every message with the bot's user id, so read-back `senderHandle` is always `U0…BOT`. The README's Mapping table omits the `senderHandle` row entirely (Discord's and Zulip's READMEs both carry it) and its 'Multiple concurrent sessions' section affirmatively says sharing one app's tokens across sessions 'is fine for the Web API half' — which is the opposite of the operational truth for presence.
failure: core/engine/presence.ts:202 keys the roster on `m.senderHandle`. Two Parley bridges configured with handles `ctx-payments` and `ctx-reviews` on one Slack app both post heartbeats that read back as sender `U0PARLEY`, so `parley_list_users` collapses them into a single phantom peer whose advertised topics are whichever beat landed last — and hand-off by handle silently targets the wrong instance. Zulip's README explicitly warns to give every session its own bot; Slack's says the opposite.
remediation: Add a `senderHandle` row to the Mapping table ('the Slack user/bot id of the poster — the logical `identity` argument is NOT carried'), and correct 'Multiple concurrent sessions' to state that sharing one bot token collapses presence/roster identity, recommending a bot per session (or a distinct app) as Zulip's README does.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'shared-account backends must declare their identity fidelity' with a cross-backend conformance case (opt-in flag on ConformanceContext, e.g. `carriesSenderIdentity`) that posts as two distinct handles and asserts either distinct read-back senderHandles (identity-carrying backends) or that the backend has declared it does not carry identity — so the seam-level fact is asserted in code, and the README claim is checkable rather than prose-only.

summary: `isPlainMessage` admits only `subtype === undefined` or `'bot_message'`, but its JSDoc claims everything excluded is 'a mutation/system record'. Slack's message subtypes include genuinely user-authored messages — notably `file_share` (a file/image posted with a comment) and `me_message` — which are silently dropped from both catch-up and live push.
failure: A human posts a screenshot with the caption 'here is the failing trace' in a mapped channel. Slack delivers it as `{type:'message', subtype:'file_share', text:'here is the failing trace', ...}`; the plugin filters it out, so the agent never sees the message via `<channel>` push or via `parley_fetch_recent` — silent data loss with no diagnostic, and the cursor advances past it.
remediation: Invert to an explicit denylist of mutation/system subtypes (`message_changed`, `message_deleted`, `channel_join`/`leave`, `channel_topic`/`purpose`/`name`, `thread_broadcast`, `tombstone`, …) and surface everything else, or add `file_share` and `me_message` to the allowlist. Either way, correct the JSDoc, which currently asserts a false universal.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'subtype classification must be enumerated, not assumed' with a table-driven case listing every Slack subtype the plugin can meet, each tagged surface|drop, run through BOTH the history path and the socket path; a new subtype added to the table without a decision fails the test, which is exactly the pressure a denylist/allowlist boundary needs.

summary: `readRetryAfter` caps the honored `Retry-After` at 5 s, and `fetchWithRetry` retries 429 in an unbounded `for(;;)` loop with no attempt cap, deadline, or abort signal. Under a sustained Slack rate limit the plugin retries far sooner than Slack asked and never gives up.
failure: Slack returns `429 Retry-After: 60` for a tiered method. The plugin waits 5 s, retries, is 429'd again, and repeats indefinitely — so a single `parley_post` / `parley_fetch_recent` MCP tool call hangs with no upper bound (only `disconnect()` breaks the loop), while ignoring the vendor's explicit backoff instruction, which risks app-level throttling escalation.
remediation: Honor the full `Retry-After` (cap far higher, e.g. 60 s, or not at all) and give `fetchWithRetry` a bounded total deadline / max attempts so a tool call fails loudly instead of hanging. If the 5 s cap is deliberate to stay under client tool timeouts, then the retry budget must be bounded by that same timeout and the call must return an error when it is exhausted.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'retry loops must terminate and must not undercut the server-instructed delay' with a parameterized case over Retry-After in {absent, '0', '1', '30', '120', 'garbage'} x a fake that 429s K times for K in {1, 3, ∞}: assert the observed inter-attempt gap is >= the instructed delay (or the documented default when absent) and that the infinite case rejects within a bounded deadline rather than hanging.

summary: The provisioning section instructs operators to grant `channels:read`, but the plugin never calls any conversations-listing/metadata method — only `chat.postMessage`, `conversations.history`, `apps.connections.open`, `auth.test` and `users.lookupByEmail`. A granted-but-unused scope widens the blast radius of a leaked `xoxb-` token (channel enumeration across the workspace) for no functional gain.
failure: An operator follows the README, grants `channels:read`, and a leaked bot token can enumerate every public channel in the workspace — a capability the bridge itself never exercises, contradicting DESIGN §14's 'no wildcard-everything by default' posture.
remediation: Drop `channels:read` from the documented scope list (keep `channels:history`, `chat:write`, and the `users:read` + `users:read.email` pair that lookupByEmail requires), and note which scope each seam method needs so the list stays auditable against the code.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'documented required scopes must equal the scopes the code exercises' with a test that inventories the Web API method names reachable from src (a simple source scan or a fake that records every method hit while driving connect/post/fetchRecent/subscribe/resolveIdentity) and asserts the set maps exactly onto the README's scope table — so adding a call or trimming a scope forces the doc to move with it.

summary: `fetchRecent` never calls `ensureTopicRouting`, so a catch-up-only (reactive/chat) deployment using an `@channelusername` topic literal never registers the numeric reverse route and every inbound message is filed under a phantom numeric topic — permanently invisible.
failure: connect({token,api_url,store_path}) with no chat_map; topic = '@mychannel'; only fetchRecent is ever called (live_push off, no post). A human posts in the channel. getUpdates delivers chat.id = -1001234567890; topicOf() finds no reverse entry and files the record under topic '-1001234567890'. Repro output: store line `{"topic":"-1001234567890",...,"content":"hi"}` while `fetchRecent({topic:'@mychannel'})` returns `[]` — forever, and across restarts because the wrong topic is persisted.
remediation: Stop keying the store/routing on the Parley topic string. Canonicalize topic -> chat id once (chat_map or literal, `@name` resolved via getChat) and index observed records by canonical chat id; have fetchRecent/subscribe/post all resolve topic -> chat id and query by chat id, so ingest ordering and which seam method ran first cannot affect what is retrievable. At minimum, call `ensureTopicRouting(topic)` from `fetchRecent` too.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a single inbound-routing table over every way a topic can name a chat — {numeric literal, '@name' literal, chat_map->numeric, chat_map->'@name', renamed chat_map key} x {first seam call = fetchRecent | subscribe | post} — asserting the injected foreign message is returned by fetchRecent(topic) and delivered to a subscriber in all cells. The existing BUG-08 tests only cover the two cells where subscribe runs first, which is why this survived.

summary: `connect` starts the shared getUpdates loop before any topic route for an `@name` topic literal exists (that route is only added later by subscribe/post), so the ~24h Telegram backlog replayed on every restart is ingested under the numeric chat id and is permanently unreachable — the store's dedup set then blocks any refiling.
failure: connect(); a human message already sits in the getUpdates backlog for @mychannel; the poll loop ingests it as topic '-1001234567890' before the bridge calls subscribe('@mychannel'). Repro: after waiting for the store file to contain the message, `plugin.subscribe('@mychannel')` then `fetchRecent({topic:'@mychannel'})` returns `[]` while the message is on disk. Later messages route correctly, so the topic silently starts mid-stream.
remediation: Resolve routing eagerly and completely before ingestion can run: either index by canonical chat id (see the sibling finding) or defer starting `pollLoop()` until routing for all configured topics is registered, and buffer/re-route updates whose chat id has no route yet.
testUpgrade: Add a startup-ordering case class: for each topic spelling, inject the foreign message BEFORE the first subscribe/post and assert it is still retrievable — a table driven by an `arriveBeforeRoute: boolean` axis added to the routing table above, plus a cold-restart repetition to prove the misfiled topic is not persisted.

summary: `observed_retention_per_topic` is applied only in the ObservedStore constructor; `append`/`insert` enforce no bound, so a long-lived bridge grows RAM and the JSONL file without limit — exactly what the BUG-32 JSDoc claims it prevents.
failure: new ObservedStore(path, 3) then 10 appends -> `store.entries('t').length === 10` and the file has 10 lines (repro printed `in-memory count after 10 appends with max 3: 10`). In production a bridge that never restarts on a busy chat accumulates every observed message in memory and on disk indefinitely; the bound only bites at the next connect.
remediation: Enforce the bound in `append`: after `insert`, if the topic list exceeds `maxPerTopic`, splice the head, drop the evicted ids from `seen`, and periodically compact the file (or rewrite on a size/eviction threshold). Also bound the number of topics retained, since the number of chats a bot is added to is attacker-controlled.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a retention-invariant test over (maxPerTopic, appendCount, topicCount) including counts far above the bound, asserting after EACH append that entries(topic).length <= max, seen.size is bounded, and on-disk lines are bounded — a property test, not a single load-time snapshot. The existing BUG-32 test only constructs a store over a pre-written file, so it can never observe the append path.

summary: `connect` never validates the token (no getMe, and `token: undefined` silently becomes ''), and the poll loop swallows every non-429 failure with a 500ms retry and zero diagnostics — a bridge with a wrong/absent token reports "bridge up" and is a silent black hole that hammers the API ~2 req/s forever.
failure: connect({api_url, store_path}) with NO token resolves in 1ms without error; cli.ts prints `parley-telegram: bridge up`; a subsequently injected message is never delivered (`live` still `[]` after 800ms in the repro) and nothing is ever written to stderr. Same shape for a revoked token (401) or a bad api_url (404).
remediation: Call `getMe()` during `connect` and throw on failure (fail-fast, and it also warms the memo used by resolveIdentity); treat missing `token` as a config error. In `pollLoop`, classify 401/403/404 as fatal (stop and surface) and write a rate-limited diagnostic to stderr for repeated failures rather than looping silently.
testUpgrade: Add a connect-preflight case class parameterized over failure modes {missing token, 401, 404, unreachable api_url}: each must reject `connect()` (or surface an error) rather than resolve; plus a poll-loop case asserting a persistent non-429 failure is reported and does not spin unboundedly. Applies to every HTTP backend, so put the shape in the conformance/contract layer.

summary: `numericChatId` mints a synthetic numeric id for ANY string, so the conformance suite runs on topics like `chat-3-a9f2` that real Telegram would reject with 400 (chat not found) — and because every conformance message is an own post ingested with the caller's topic, the topic->chat->topic round trip is never exercised at all.
failure: runConformanceSuite('telegram') passes 8/8 while `fetchRecent` on a real `@name` or numeric-chat deployment returns nothing for inbound messages (see the two routing findings). Mutation check: deleting `ensureTopicRouting` entirely, or making `topicOf` return `asTopic('x')`, keeps the whole conformance suite green.
remediation: Make the fake reject chat_id values that are not `^-?\d+$` or `^@[A-Za-z0-9_]{5,}$` with 400, and have the telegram conformance context mint `freshTopic()` as a numeric chat id (or a chat_map-backed friendly name). Add a conformance/plugin hook that injects a FOREIGN message so every backend's inbound path is covered by the shared suite, not only by per-plugin tests.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "fake accepts what the vendor rejects": table-drive the fake's chat_id validation (valid numeric / valid @name / invalid literal -> 400) and assert the plugin surfaces the 400; and widen the conformance context with an optional `injectForeign(topic)` so the round trip topic -> backend channel -> topic is asserted for every backend that has one.

summary: `fetchRecent` with `limit: 0` returns the ENTIRE topic history when `since` is omitted (`all.slice(-0)` === `all.slice(0)`), but an empty page when `since` is set — the same argument means opposite things; negative limits drop leading messages.
failure: post 'a','b' then `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 0})` -> `['a','b']` (repro output `limit 0 -> [ 'a', 'b' ]`), while `fetchRecent({topic, since:'0', limit: 0})` -> `[]`. `limit: -5` returns `all.slice(5)`.
remediation: Normalize once at the top: `const limit = Math.max(0, Math.floor(args.limit ?? 100))` and slice with an explicit start index (`all.slice(Math.max(0, all.length - limit))`) so limit 0 means "no messages" on both branches. Core's zod `positive()` guard means only direct seam callers hit this, which is precisely who the seam contract is for.
testUpgrade: Add a shared conformance case parameterized over limit values {0, 1, negative, > total, undefined} x {since set, since omitted} asserting `messages.length <= max(0, limit)` and a monotonic non-regressing nextCursor — it would catch this class in any backend that hand-rolls slicing.

summary: `ingest` records `msg.text ?? ''` for every `message`/`channel_post`, so a photo, sticker, document, voice note or a captioned image becomes a message with empty content that is persisted, pushed to the agent, and advances the topic cursor — `caption` is never read and non-text updates are never skipped.
failure: A human sends a photo with caption "deploy this" to a subscribed chat: the agent receives a `<channel>` message with `content: ''`, and `fetchRecent` replays a blank line. The caption text is silently dropped.
remediation: Read `msg.caption` as a fallback for `text`, and for payloads with neither, either skip ingestion or synthesize an explicit placeholder (e.g. `[photo]`) so the agent is not handed a blank turn. Document whichever is chosen in the README seam-mapping table.
testUpgrade: Table-drive an update-shape fixture set {text, caption+photo, sticker, document, empty} through the fake's inject path and assert the normalized content for each — a widened generator over Telegram Message variants, not just the `text` happy path currently exercised.

summary: The shared poll loop ingests and durably persists every message from every chat the bot is in, under a topic derived from the chat id — with no allowlist filter and (per the retention finding) no per-topic count bound at runtime and no bound on the number of topics.
failure: Anyone who can add the bot to a group (or a compromised group member) can drive unbounded writes into the operator's `store_path` — arbitrary attacker-controlled text persisted to the operator's disk in a chat the operator never configured, growing until the filesystem fills.
remediation: Give the plugin the set of chat ids it actually serves (derived from configured topics/chat_map) and drop updates from unknown chats without persisting them; keep a small bounded counter for observability instead of records. Combine with an append-path retention bound and a cap on the number of retained topics.
testUpgrade: Add a case class "ingest of an unconfigured chat": inject messages for a chat id that is neither in chat_map nor any subscribed/fetched topic and assert no store growth; parameterize over {unknown numeric chat, unknown @name channel, high-volume flood} so any future ingest path is covered.

summary: `parseCompositeMid` discards the chat half of `<chat_id>:<message_id>`, so an `inReplyTo` produced in a DIFFERENT chat is used verbatim as `reply_to_message_id` in this chat.
failure: post(topicA, h, 'x', { inReplyTo: '<chatB>:7' }) sends `reply_to_message_id: 7` to chat A — either a 400 from Telegram (post fails for a reason the caller cannot diagnose) or, if chat A happens to have a message 7, a reply threaded onto an unrelated message.
remediation: Parse both halves; only set `reply_to_message_id` when the chat half equals the canonical chat id for `topic`, otherwise ignore it (or throw a clear error). Also require the message-id half to be a positive integer.
testUpgrade: Parameterize an inReplyTo table over {same-chat composite, other-chat composite, non-composite string, negative/NaN mid, empty} asserting the outgoing sendMessage body for each — guards every backend that parses a composite backendMsgId.

summary: `this.ingest(...)` runs OUTSIDE the poll loop's try/catch, and `pollLoop()` is started with a bare `void` and no `.catch`, so any throw from ingest (e.g. `appendFileSync` hitting ENOSPC/EIO/EBADF) terminates ingestion permanently and surfaces as an unhandled rejection — which Node 22 turns into process exit.
failure: Disk fills while the bridge runs: the next `appendFileSync` throws inside `ingest`, the getUpdates loop exits, live push and every parked `fetch_recent` long-poll go dead silently (or the whole MCP server dies with an unhandled rejection), and the already-fetched updates are never acknowledged.
remediation: Wrap the per-update processing in try/catch, log to stderr, and continue; attach a `.catch` to `void this.pollLoop()` that reports and either restarts the loop with backoff or marks the plugin failed. Have `ObservedStore.append` surface write failures as a boolean/error rather than propagating raw fs exceptions into the loop.
testUpgrade: Add a fault-injection case class: stub the store's append (and the message handler) to throw, then assert the loop keeps consuming subsequent updates and no unhandled rejection is emitted — parameterized over the throw site {store append, handler, topicOf} so the guard cannot regress at a new site.

summary: The README's `backend_config` table lists 5 keys and omits `observed_retention_per_topic`, which the code accepts and whose default (10000) silently bounds how much history `fetchRecent` can replay — the one thing this backend's README spends a whole section promising.
failure: An operator reading the README believes the observed store keeps everything it has seen; after 10000 messages in a chat the oldest observations are dropped on the next connect (the file is compacted, so they are gone from disk too) with no documented knob to raise the bound.
remediation: Add the row (default 10000, semantics = newest-N per topic, enforced at load and — once fixed — on append, with the compaction side effect) and cross-reference it from the "History limitations" section.
testUpgrade: Add a docs-vs-code check that parses the `TelegramBackendConfig` interface keys and asserts each appears in the README config table (and vice versa) — run it for every plugin so the class 'shipped knob absent from the documented table' cannot recur under a new name.

summary: README and the poll-loop comment state that HTTP 409 means "another getUpdates consumer holds this token", but Telegram also returns 409 when a webhook is registered for the bot — a state that never self-heals, yet the plugin retries it every 3s forever and the provisioning section never tells the operator to call deleteWebhook.
failure: An operator who previously configured a webhook for the bot starts the bridge: getUpdates returns 409 ("can't use getUpdates method while webhook is active") indefinitely; the bridge reports up, delivers nothing, and both the code comment and README point the operator at the wrong diagnosis (a phantom second bridge).
remediation: Document both causes in the README (add `deleteWebhook` to the provisioning steps) and either call deleteWebhook at connect (opt-in) or surface the 409 description text to stderr so the operator sees Telegram's own explanation instead of a silent retry.
testUpgrade: Add a fake-server case class for terminal-vs-transient error codes {409 webhook, 409 conflict, 401, 429}: assert the plugin's observable reaction (retry cadence, diagnostic emitted, fatal vs not) per code, so any error-code claim in prose is backed by an executed branch.

summary: 429 loop has no attempt cap, deadline or escalation; a permanently-429 backend hangs the MCP call forever, bypassing catchup.block_max_ms.

The 'MUST cap at 5000, default 500' backoff contract is JSDoc delegated to five plugin parsers; fetchWithRetry clamps nothing, so retryAfterOf()=>0 gives ~850 req/s against the operator's own account.

Non-2xx path reads the whole body and embeds it verbatim in the Error, which becomes an isError tool result: 5MB body -> 5,000,009-char message, and a prompt-injection path that bypasses the untrusted-message framing.
Suite never passes a truncating limit, so nextCursor=topic-tail passes. 250 messages + limit 100 silently loses 150.
Only content/backendMsgId/cursor asserted; constant senderHandle and constant topic both pass. Constant topic collapses the dedup namespace across topics.
Live case posts one message to a fresh topic, so neither ascending-cursor order nor no-history-replay is testable. Reversed delivery passes; replay-from-0 (BUG-11) passes.
README/JSDoc/npm description say HTTP backends only; redis, postgres and xmpp all import delay from it. 8 of 10 backends depend on it.
Claims five backends are verified; ten are. Its copied ConformanceContext omits supportsBlockingFetch, so a new author silently loses the blocking-fetch case.
supportsBlockingFetch/concurrentPost are opt-in, so forgetting them silently reduces coverage instead of failing.
resolveIdentity, one of the six seam methods, is never called by the suite.
seam.ts permits NoSuchTopicError for an absent topic; the suite hard-requires an empty page, so the documented alternative fails conformance. No plugin implements it.
isStopped is checked only after a response, so a disconnect during backoff still costs one more request with torn-down credentials; delay is not abortable or unref'd.
'waits precisely the caller-supplied backoff' measures no time; it certifies the hot-loop behaviour of the clamp finding.
All five readRetryAfter implementations share a byte-identical header/clamp/default prologue; only the body field differs. BUG-41 had to be fixed five times.
include is src/** only, so the package's only test file is never typechecked by npm run build.
The only published package with no keywords at all, and its exports omit ./package.json.
The conformance package ships zero tests of its own; vitest exits 1 with 'No test files found'.
drainAll(.., expectedAtMost) passes straight through as fetchRecent's limit and reads exactly one page; it does not drain.
